Paul takes Peter's mixed-table practice as the position consistent with the truth of the gospel, and treats the withdrawal as the deviation from it. Whatever "living like a Gentile" meant in practice — and the text does not tell us how far it went — Paul regarded it as the correct behaviour of a Jewish apostle among Gentile believers.
Second half: pōs ta ethnē anankazeis ioudaizein — "how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?"

The verb ioudaizō means to adopt Jewish practice, to live as a Jew. Its most instructive occurrence anywhere is Esther 8:17 in the Greek version, which describes what happened after Mordecai's elevation: "and many of the Gentiles were circumcised and Judaized (perietemnonto kai ioudaizon) for fear of the Jews." There the verb is paired directly with circumcision and describes Gentiles taking on Jewish identity under pressure. That is exactly the situation Paul is describing, including the pressure.

How the charge works. Peter has issued no command. He has not told anyone to be circumcised. Paul's accusation is nevertheless "you are compelling," and the logic is worth making explicit because it is the letter's most concrete illustration of what it is arguing against.

When the senior apostle withdraws from the common table, the Gentile believers are not merely inconvenienced. They are placed outside the fellowship of the community's recognized leadership. There remains exactly one route back to full inclusion, and it runs through becoming Jews. No one has to say so. The structure of the situation says it.

That is why the verb is anankazō, "compel" — the same verb used of Titus at 2:3 and of the Galatian teachers at 6:12. Pressure exerted by circumstance is what the letter opposes, and Paul is prepared to name a friend's social withdrawal as an instance of it.

div.title: Verses 15-16: What Jews Know

div.p: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet knowing that a person is not justified by works of law but through faith of Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, in order that we might be justified by faith of Christ and not by works of law, because by works of law no flesh will be justified.

This sentence is the hinge of the letter. Everything before it is narrative; everything after it is argument. It also contains three expressions whose meaning is contested and on which the reading of the entire letter turns. Each is set out below with the evidence available for deciding it.

p.hi: Verse 15: "We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners."

div.p: Hēmeis physei Ioudaioi kai ouk ex ethnōn hamartōloi. Physei means "by nature, by birth" — Jews by descent rather than by conversion, which is a distinction that matters in a letter about proselytes.

"Gentile sinners" is the insider's idiom, and Paul uses it without softening. In this usage a Gentile is a "sinner" by definition and by category rather than by conduct: outside the covenant, without the Torah, and therefore not living the ordered life the Torah sets out. The usage is well attested: "they fell into the hands of the Gentiles" is paralleled with sinners at 1 Maccabees 2:44 ("they struck down sinners in their anger and lawless men in their wrath"); the Psalms of Solomon set "sinners" against the righteous of Israel (1:1; 2:1-2); and the Gospels preserve the pairing "tax collectors and sinners."
Paul quotes the category and then, two verses later, destabilizes it: at 2:17 "we ourselves were found to be sinners." The sentence is built to be undermined.

p.hi: Verse 16, first term: erga nomou, "works of law."

div.p: The phrase appears three times in this verse — it is the most repeated expression in the sentence — and it is the letter's central contested term. Two readings are current, and the evidence for each should be stated fairly.

Reading one: the practices that mark the boundary between Jew and Gentile. On this account, "works of law" denotes not obedience in general but the observances by which Jewish identity is publicly maintained — circumcision, food laws, sabbath and festival calendar.

The evidence: a document from Qumran, conventionally called 4QMMT, uses the Hebrew phrase miqsat ma'ase ha-torah, "some of the works of the Torah," for a specific set of halakhic rulings on purity, sacrifice and marriage that distinguish the writers' practice from that of their opponents. The phrase in a first-century Jewish setting is thus attested for a defined subset of Torah practice functioning as a boundary, rather than for obedience as a whole. Supporting this from the letter itself: the presenting issues in Galatia are circumcision (2:3; 5:2-3; 6:12-13), table fellowship (2:11-14) and calendar (4:10) — which is to say, precisely the boundary markers, and precisely the matters at stake in the scene that has just been narrated.
Reading two: Torah-doing in general. On this account, "works of law" means anything done in obedience to the law considered as a basis for standing before God.

The evidence: at 3:10 Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 with its reference to "all things written in the book of the law," which is not a subset; and at 5:3 he says the circumcised man is a debtor "to do the whole law," which likewise embraces everything.

The two readings are not always as far apart as the debate suggests, since on either account what Paul opposes is a route to standing rather than obedience as such. But they diverge in what they imply about the letter's scope, and the reader should decide deliberately rather than by default.

p.hi: Verse 16, second term: dikaioō, "to justify."

div.p: In the Greek scriptures this is a courtroom word. It means to declare in the right, to give a favourable verdict, to acquit — and it is emphatically not a word for making someone good.

The usage is clearest where a judicial setting is explicit. "You shall not justify (dikaiōseis) the wicked for a bribe" (Exodus 23:7). Of judges: "they shall justify the righteous and condemn the guilty" (Deuteronomy 25:1) — where the pairing with condemnation makes the forensic sense unmistakable. "Woe to those who justify the wicked for a bribe and take away the justice of the righteous" (Isaiah 5:23). "He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD" (Proverbs 17:15). In none of these does the verb mean to make a wicked man good; it means to pronounce him in the right, which is exactly why doing it wrongly is an abomination.
So to be "justified" is to have a verdict pronounced in one's favour: to be reckoned, declared, counted as being in the right.

What the verse does not specify is when. Paul uses this vocabulary in both directions elsewhere — as accomplished ("having been justified by faith, we have peace with God," Romans 5:1) and as awaited ("the doers of the law will be justified," Romans 2:13; and in this letter, "we await the hope of righteousness," Galatians 5:5). Whether the verdict in view at 2:16 is a present reckoning of who belongs to God's people or a final acquittal at the end is not stated here, and the letter does not resolve it in one direction.

p.hi: Verse 16, third term: pistis Iēsou Christou, "faith of Jesus Christ."

div.p: The Greek is a genitive construction, and Greek genitives are ambiguous in a way English possessives are not. The phrase can mean:
Faith directed toward Jesus Christ — an objective genitive, where Christ is the object of the believer's trust. This is the traditional English rendering, "faith in Jesus Christ."
The faithfulness of Jesus Christ — a subjective genitive, where Christ is the one who is faithful, and his faithfulness is what secures the verdict.

There is a structural argument for the second, and it lies inside this verse. Paul writes: "even we believed in Christ Jesus (kai hēmeis eis Christon Iēsoun episteusamen), in order that we might be justified ek pisteōs Christou." On the objective reading, that sentence says: we believed in Christ in order to be justified by believing in Christ — which is circular, and an odd thing to write. On the subjective reading it says: we believed, in order to be justified by his faithfulness — which is not circular and gives the clause something to do.

The argument on the other side is that Paul uses the verb "believe" with Christ as its object without difficulty, and that at 3:6-9 he develops Abraham's own act of believing as the model, which suits a reading in which the believer's faith is in view.

A third position holds that the alternatives are less separable than the debate implies. The Greek pistis renders the Hebrew emunah in the scriptures, and emunah covers trust and steadfast reliability without a seam between them — it is used of a person's faithfulness and of their trust in God, and Hebrew does not partition the two. On this account the question "whose faith?" imposes a division the underlying category does not make. It is worth noting in this connection that at 3:11 Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4, where the Greek version reads "by my faithfulness" (God's) and the Hebrew reads "by his faithfulness" (the righteous person's) — and Paul drops the pronoun, quoting it simply as "by faith." He had two disambiguating options in front of him and took neither.

p.hi: The citation at the end of the verse, and Paul's modification of it.

div.p: The last clause is scriptural: hoti ex ergōn nomou ou dikaiōthēsetai pasa sarx.
Psalm 143:2 (LXX 142:2) reads: "for no living thing (pas zōn) will be justified before you."
Paul writes: "because by works of law no flesh will be justified."

Two changes. He has inserted ex ergōn nomou, which is not in the Psalm at all — the Psalm's statement was a general one about creatures before God and had nothing to do with law. And he has changed "living thing" to sarx, "flesh," which is a word this letter uses repeatedly for circumcision itself: "having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by flesh?" (3:3); "they want to make a good showing in the flesh... that they may boast in your flesh" (6:12-13).

Whether the second change is deliberate wordplay is not certain and should not be pressed hard. The first is unquestionably deliberate, and it is the first of four adapted citations in this letter (see also 3:10, 3:11, 3:13 and 4:30). Paul is a writer who reshapes the texts he quotes so that they bear on the argument at hand, and a reader who checks his citations against their sources will find this consistently.

One feature of the verse that any reading must account for. The first person plural is sustained and emphatic throughout: we are Jews by birth, we know this, even we believed, in order that we might be justified. Whatever the sentence claims about works of law and justification, it claims it about Paul and Peter — about Jews — and not only about the Gentiles under pressure at Antioch. Readings that treat "not by works of law" as concerning Gentile admission alone have to say what this run of pronouns is doing.

div.title: Verses 17-21: Died to Law, Alive to God

div.p: But if, in seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not! For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor. For through law I died to law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through law, then Christ died for nothing.

p.hi: Verse 17: "But if, in seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!"

div.p: Hamartōloi ("sinners") is the word from verse 15, where it designated Gentiles as a category. Paul now applies it to "we ourselves" — the Jews of verse 15.

The observation being made is sharp. In seeking to be reckoned right in Christ, Jews have placed themselves in the position they had assigned to Gentiles: needing a verdict they do not possess by birth. The line that separated the two groups has collapsed at exactly the point where justification is in view. And in the immediate context of Antioch there is a further edge: by eating with Gentiles, Peter had been living in a way his own tradition would have called the way of a "sinner."

The objection Paul raises against himself — ara Christos hamartias diakonos ("is Christ then a servant of sin?") — is the natural retort of someone defending the separation: if being in Christ puts a Jew in the sinners' category, then Christ is in the business of promoting sin.

Mē genoito is Paul's strongest negation, an optative construction that has no smooth English equivalent; "may it never be," "God forbid," "certainly not" all approximate it. He uses it fourteen times, ten of them in Romans, always to reject an inference drawn from his own position. It recurs in this letter at 3:21 and 6:14.

p.hi: Verse 18: "For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor."

div.p: The metaphor is construction: what was demolished (katelysa) might be built again (oikodomō).

What was torn down is not named, and the immediate context supplies the most economical answer: the separation between Jewish and Gentile believers at the common table. It had been dismantled in Antioch — Peter had been eating with Gentiles as a settled practice — and Peter's withdrawal reconstructs it.

Parabatēn emauton synistanō ("I establish myself a transgressor"). Parabatēs is a legal term formed from parabainō, "to step across" — one who crosses a line, a lawbreaker. It is not a general word for a sinner but a specific word for someone who violates a stated boundary.

The claim is arresting on any reading of the passage, and it should be allowed to be arresting. The act that constitutes the transgression is the reimposition of the separation, not its abandonment. The man who is defending Jewish practice in this letter says that rebuilding this particular wall would make him the lawbreaker.

p.hi: Verse 19: "For through law I died to law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ."

div.p: Egō gar dia nomou nomō apethanon hina theō zēsō.

The sentence turns on its first preposition. It was dia nomou, "through law," that the death to law occurred. Whatever this death is, the law was the instrument of it — not the obstacle to it, not the thing escaped from by some other route, but the means.
Two readings of that instrumentality are available in the letter.

The law's own sentence was the instrument. At 3:13 Paul will say that Christ "became a curse for us," citing Deuteronomy 21:23 — so the law's own curse provision is what fell, and the claim it had is thereby discharged. On this reading, the law ended its hold by its own terms rather than by being set aside.

The law's own witness pointed beyond itself. On this reading, attending to what the law said led Paul out from under it — an argument the letter makes in a different form at 4:21 ("you who want to be under law, do you not hear the law?").
Then: Christō synestaurōmai — "I have been crucified with Christ."
Two features of this clause carry the weight.

The tense is perfect, which in Greek describes a completed action whose result stands. The crucifixion is not something Paul underwent repeatedly or is undergoing; it happened, and its effect is his present condition.

The verb is a compound: syn- ("with, together with") + stauroō ("to crucify"). The death is therefore participatory, not parallel. Paul is not saying that he died in a manner resembling Christ's death, or that he died as a result of it. He is saying that he was in it.

A word about what crucifixion was, since the metaphor loses its force if the reality behind it is unfamiliar. It was a Roman method of public execution reserved for slaves, rebels and non-citizens. The condemned was fixed to a beam and left in the open to die slowly of exhaustion and asphyxiation, in view of passers-by, often for days, and frequently left unburied afterward. Its purpose was as much deterrence as punishment, and it carried a stigma that made it nearly unmentionable in polite Roman writing. Paul uses it as the image for his own relation to the law and, at 5:24 and 6:14, for the believer's relation to the flesh and to the world.

What "dying to law" can and cannot mean. The letter itself supplies a control on this, and it comes at 4:4-5, where Christ is described as "born under law (hypo nomon), so that he might redeem those under law." Since Christ observed Torah, "under law" in that verse cannot be a description of Torah practice — the sentence would otherwise say that he needed rescuing from his own faithfulness. It must denote a standing or jurisdiction: being within the law's authority and subject to its sanctions.

That bears directly on 2:19. If "under law" names a jurisdiction rather than a practice, then "dying to law" most naturally names the end of that jurisdiction rather than the abandonment of the practice. The verse does not say which, and readers should note that the control comes from two chapters later rather than from here.

p.hi: Verse 20: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

div.p: The paradox is stated in three moves and it is not resolved: I no longer live; Christ lives in me; and yet I do live, in the flesh.

Ho de nyn zō en sarki ("what I now live in flesh") uses sarx in its plain sense of bodily existence — ordinary embodied life, without any of the polemical charge the word carries at 3:3 or 6:12-13. The same word does very different work in different places in this letter, and the reader should not import one sense into another.

En pistei zō tē tou huiou tou theou ("I live by faith of the Son of God") repeats the ambiguous genitive of 2:16, and the same options apply. Some early manuscripts, including the third-century P46 and Codex Vaticanus, read "faith of God and Christ" instead of "faith of the Son of God."

The verse closes with two participles: tou agapēsantos me kai paradontos heauton hyper emou — "who loved me and gave himself for me." Both are singular, and this is the only place in the letter where Paul puts the cross in the first person singular. The greeting had it in the plural: "who gave himself for our sins" (1:4). Here, in the middle of an argument about Jews and Gentiles and covenants and jurisdiction, it contracts to one person.

p.hi: Verse 21: "I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through law, then Christ died for nothing."

div.p: Ouk athetō tēn charin tou theou ("I do not set aside the grace of God"). Atheteō means "to render void, to set aside, to reject as invalid" — it is used of annulling an agreement. The denial implies an accusation: someone has said that Paul's position nullifies something. He answers by returning the charge, and the conditional that follows identifies which position actually does the nullifying.
Ei gar dia nomou dikaiosynē, ara Christos dōrean apethanen — "for if righteousness is through law, then Christ died gratuitously."

Dōrean is the adverb of dōron, "gift." It means "as a gift, freely" and, by extension, "for nothing, without cause, to no purpose." The same word appears at Romans 3:24 in the positive sense (justified "freely by his grace") and at John 15:25 in the negative ("they hated me without cause").

The form of the argument matters as much as its content. This is a reductio: assume the proposition, and an unacceptable consequence follows. And it is worth noting precisely what Paul does not argue here.
He does not say the law is bad.
He does not say that no one keeps the law.
He does not say the law was a failed attempt at something.

He says that if righteousness comes by that route, then one thing follows: the death was purposeless. The argument runs on the incompatibility of two routes to the same thing, not on the deficiency of one of them.

The positive counterpart to this negative statement arrives at 3:21, and the two verses should be read together: "if a law had been given that was able to make alive, then righteousness would indeed have been by law." No such law was given. The law is not opposed to the promise; it was not issued to do the promise's work. That is a claim about the law's remit, and it is the letter's own answer to the question this verse raises.

div.title: The Chapter's Argument as a Whole

list.item: The two scenes are structured as opposites, and both serve one point. In Jerusalem, Paul's gospel is examined and confirmed, and the leadership adds nothing. In Antioch, Paul confronts one of the men who confirmed it. Together they establish a position that neither scene could establish alone: Paul's message is not derived from Jerusalem, and it is not at odds with Jerusalem — and when Antioch practice diverged from what Jerusalem had agreed, it was Paul who held the line.

What was decided about Titus is narrow and load-bearing. An uncircumcised Greek was in the room, and he "was not compelled to be circumcised." The agreement that followed divided mission fields, not gospels — one message, two spheres, sealed by a handshake. And the only obligation laid on the Gentile mission was to remember the poor. At the meeting where the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews, the answer imposed one requirement and it was charitable.

The Antioch dispute concerns who may eat together, and the distinction from what may be eaten is decisive. The written Torah regulates food; it contains no commandment against Gentile company. The restriction Peter honours is called athemiton in his own mouth at Acts 10:28 — a word for custom, with no commandment cited, because there is none. This is what allows Paul to describe Peter's earlier practice approvingly and to call the withdrawal hypocrisy rather than obedience.

The charge against Peter is that circumstance can function as compulsion. Peter commands nothing. But a senior apostle's withdrawal leaves Gentile believers outside the fellowship of the leadership with exactly one route back, and that route is conversion. The verb anankazō ("compel") is used of this, and it is the same verb used of Titus at 2:3 and of the Galatian teachers at 6:12 — the letter's three instances of pressure applied to Gentiles.

Paul states Peter's mixed-table practice as the premise of the rebuke, not as part of the offence. "If you, being a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew" is said without censure; it is the ground from which the accusation proceeds. Whatever it meant in practice, Paul treats it as consistent with the truth of the gospel and treats the withdrawal as the deviation.

2:15-16 presents its central claim as shared knowledge rather than as news. "Knowing that a person is not justified by works of law" states a premise Paul expects to be granted, from which Peter's conduct is then shown to deviate. He is not instructing a Jewish apostle in something novel; he is holding him to something both already hold.

The first person plural in 2:15-16 is sustained, and it is the chapter's hardest datum. "We are Jews by birth... even we believed... that we might be justified." Whatever the sentence claims, it claims about Jews, including Paul. Any reading that confines the issue to how Gentiles are admitted must account for these pronouns.

Three decisions in 2:16 govern the rest of the letter, and none of them is settled by the verse. What erga nomou denotes — the boundary-marking observances, on the analogy of 4QMMT's "some of the works of the Torah," or Torah-doing as such. Whether dikaioō names a present reckoning or a final verdict, since Paul uses it in both directions. And whether pistis Iēsou Christou means faith directed toward Christ, Christ's own faithfulness, or a term that does not divide that way, given that the underlying Hebrew emunah does not. The evidence for each has been set out above; the verse does not adjudicate, and readings of the letter diverge accordingly.

Paul reshapes the scripture he cites, and this is the first of several instances. Psalm 143:2 says no living thing will be justified before God. Paul writes that no flesh will be justified by works of law, inserting the phrase that makes the citation bear on his argument. The Psalm did not concern law; in his hand it does. The same practice appears at 3:10, 3:11, 3:13 and 4:30, and a reader who checks the citations will find it consistently.

2:19-20 describes the death as participatory, and 2:21 argues by reductio. Paul does not say he abandoned the law; he says he died to it, through it, and that the death was a crucifixion with Christ — a compound verb in the perfect tense, a completed event whose effect is his present condition. And he does not argue that law-righteousness fails because nobody achieves it. He argues that if it were available, the death would have been pointless. The positive form of the same claim is at 3:21: no law able to make alive was given.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: Where this stands in the letter: Chapters 1 and 2 were autobiography deployed as argument — Paul's commission, his distance from Jerusalem, the meeting there, and the confrontation at Antioch. At 2:15 the letter turned from narrative to argument, and chapter 3 carries that argument in two registers, in this order: first from what the Galatians themselves experienced (3:1-5), then from scripture (3:6-29).

The order matters. Paul had already ruled out arguing from his own authority when he pronounced a curse on himself, hypothetically, at 1:8. What remains available to him is evidence, and he begins with the evidence his readers can check without consulting anyone.

The chapter's question. Underneath the presenting dispute lies a single question: who counts as Abraham's offspring? This is not a side issue. The promises that matter — land, descendants, blessing to the nations — were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and inheriting them depends on being counted among them. Circumcision is the sign given to Abraham in Genesis 17 and given specifically as the covenant sign for him and his descendants. So a Gentile who wants to belong to Abraham's family has an obvious route in front of him, and the teachers in Galatia appear to have been pointing to it.

Paul's counter-move is to go two chapters earlier in the same narrative. In Genesis 15, before any sign is instituted, Abraham believes God and it is reckoned to him as righteousness. Paul builds his case from there.

The chapter is built on six scriptural citations, and he adapts several of them. Genesis 15:6 at 3:6; Genesis 12:3 and 18:18 conflated at 3:8; Deuteronomy 27:26 at 3:10; Habakkuk 2:4 at 3:11; Leviticus 18:5 at 3:12; Deuteronomy 21:23 at 3:13. The argument's force comes from setting these against one another, and three of the six are quoted in a form that differs from the sources. Those differences are set out in the comments below, because they are not incidental — in each case the change is what makes the citation bear on the argument.

What the author argues immediately after (Galatians 4): Chapter 4 continues without a break, extending the household metaphor of 3:23-25: the minor heir under guardians comes of age at the date his father set (4:1-7). Paul then applies the argument to the Galatians' present situation with a sharp warning (4:8-11), abandons argument for personal appeal (4:12-20), and closes with an allegory of Hagar and Sarah that restates the whole case in narrative form (4:21-31).

How chapter 3 connects to what follows: The connections are tight and verbal. The paidagogos of 3:24-25 becomes the guardians and stewards of 4:2. The release from the paidagogos becomes the heir's coming of age. The "sons of God" of 3:26 becomes the adoption of 4:5 and the Abba cry of 4:6. The "heirs according to promise" of 3:29 becomes "no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir" at 4:7. Chapters 3 and 4 are a single movement and should be read as one.

div.title: Verses 1-5: The Argument from Their Own Experience

div.p: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly placarded as crucified? This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of law or by a hearing of faith? Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by flesh? Did you experience so many things in vain — if indeed it was in vain? Does he then who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of law, or by a hearing of faith?

p.hi: Verse 1: "O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly placarded as crucified?"

div.p: Anoetoi is built on a-, "not," and noeō, "to perceive with the mind, to understand." It is a charge of failing to think, not of lacking information. Paul repeats it two verses later.

"Who has bewitched you?" is tis hymas ebaskanen, from baskainō. This verb belongs to the world of the evil eye, and the belief behind it needs stating for a reader to whom it is unfamiliar, because Paul has chosen the image deliberately.

Across the ancient Mediterranean, and in Jewish sources as well as Greek and Roman ones, it was widely believed that a person could be harmed by another's malicious or envious look. The gaze itself was thought to carry the injury — particularly the gaze of the envious upon someone flourishing. Protective amulets against the evil eye are among the commonest surviving small objects from the period. The Greek scriptures use the related expression at Deuteronomy 15:9 and 28:54, and Proverbs 23:6 and 28:22 warn against the man with a "grudging eye." The verb baskainō is the technical term for casting it.

Paul is not making a literal charge of sorcery; the question is rhetorical and it stings. But the image is chosen for what it sets up. The Galatians have been affected by a look — and Paul immediately reminds them of a very different thing that was set before their eyes.

Hois kat' ophthalmous Iēsous Christos proegraphē estaurōmenos. The verb prographō combines pro ("before, in front of, publicly") with graphō ("to write"). It can mean "to write beforehand," but its other and more vivid sense is "to post up publicly, to placard" — the language of a public notice fixed where everyone can read it, an edict or a proclamation displayed in the open.
That is the contrast Paul is drawing. Against a covert glance that harms, a public placard that anyone may read; against the evil eye, an event set out in the open before their eyes.

The participle estaurōmenos is perfect passive: "having been crucified," a completed action whose result stands. Not the event of the crucifixion but the crucified one as an abiding reality. And the placard, on this image, was Paul's own preaching — he had put the crucified Christ up in front of them where they could see him.

p.hi: Verse 2: "This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of law or by a hearing of faith?"

div.p: The whole paragraph turns on one question, asked twice (here and at verse 5), and it is a question about something that happened to the readers.

Notice the method. Paul does not begin from scripture — that comes at verse 6. He does not begin from his apostolic standing — he has forfeited that as a criterion at 1:8. He begins from an event the Galatians can attest without anyone's help: they received the Spirit. Whatever that consisted of in their experience, verse 5 indicates it included visible phenomena, and it is treated throughout as something nobody in the conversation disputes.
Touto monon thelō mathein aph' hymōn ("this only I want to learn from you") is a debating posture: I concede everything else and ask one thing.
Ex akoēs pisteōs ("by a hearing of faith") is ambiguous in both of its nouns, and the ambiguity should be reported rather than resolved by translation.

Akoē can mean the act of hearing, or the thing heard — a report, a message. The second sense is the one in Isaiah 53:1 in the Greek: tis episteusen tē akoē hēmōn, "who has believed our report?" Paul quotes that verse at Romans 10:16 and then glosses it in the next verse: "so faith comes from hearing (akoēs), and hearing through the word of Christ."
Pisteōs is a genitive and may indicate source ("hearing that springs from faith"), content ("the message about faith"), or description ("believing hearing").

The phrase therefore might be rendered "by hearing with faith," "by the message of faith," or "by believing what you heard." What carries the argument is the contrast, and the contrast survives every resolution of the ambiguity: on one side something done, on the other something heard.

p.hi: Verse 3: "Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by flesh?"

div.p: Enarxamenoi pneumati nyn sarki epiteleisthe. The two verbs are a matched pair, and both belong to the vocabulary of religious rites: enarchomai, "to begin, to make the initial offering, to inaugurate," and epiteleō, "to complete, to bring to its proper end, to perform fully." Both are used in Greek of the beginning and completion of a sacred action. The question is therefore about a single process: something inaugurated in one medium and now being finished in another.
Sarx, "flesh," appears here for the first time in the letter's argument, and it is the letter's most flexible and most loaded word. Its range in Galatians:

list.item: plain bodily existence, with no negative charge: "the life I now live in the flesh" (2:20); "a weakness of the flesh" (4:13)
human descent or human contrivance: Ishmael "born according to flesh" (4:23, 29)
the disordered self in its opposition to the Spirit: the "works of the flesh" (5:19-21), "crucified the flesh" (5:24)
and, specifically in this letter's polemic, circumcision — the operation performed on the flesh: "that they may make a good showing in the flesh... that they may boast in your flesh" (6:12-13)

div.p: In a chapter about whether Gentile believers should undergo circumcision, that last sense is difficult to exclude here, and the sentence would then read with a bite that translations tend to lose: you began with the Spirit; are you now being brought to completion by a surgical procedure?

p.hi: Verse 4: "Did you experience so many things in vain — if indeed it was in vain?"

div.p: Tosauta epathete. The verb paschō most often means "to suffer," and it may mean that here — pointing to persecution the Galatians had undergone. But the verb can also be neutral, "to undergo, to experience," and the surrounding verses are about the Spirit and about miracles rather than about hardship, which may indicate that what they "experienced" is what verses 2 and 5 describe.
Eikē means "without cause, to no purpose, in vain."

Then Paul corrects himself: ei ge kai eikē — "if indeed it really was in vain." He raises the possibility that everything they experienced has come to nothing and immediately declines to assert it. This mid-sentence retraction is characteristic of the letter's whole posture: the situation is grave and it is not over.

p.hi: Verse 5: "Does he then who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of law, or by a hearing of faith?"

div.p: The question of verse 2 returns with two changes.

The tense. Both participles are present: ho epichorēgōn ("the one supplying") and energōn ("working"). Verse 2 asked about the beginning; verse 5 asks about now. The Spirit is not only how they started; it is what is currently happening among them.
The addition. Dynameis, "acts of power, mighty works, miracles," is named alongside the Spirit. Whatever the Galatian congregations were experiencing, Paul can appeal to it as public and undisputed.

Epichorēgeō is worth a note because the word has a history. A chorēgos in classical Athens was a wealthy citizen assigned the public duty of financing a chorus for a dramatic festival — paying for the training, the costumes, the whole production, out of his own pocket, as a civic honour. The verb came to mean supplying generously and at one's own cost. The compound adds epi-, intensifying it further. God is pictured as bearing the whole expense.

The form of the argument, and why it comes first. Verses 2 and 5 pose the same disjunction twice, and it is an argument from evidence rather than from authority. The Spirit came among these Gentile congregations before any question of circumcision arose, and it is still at work. Whatever standing the teachers are offering to confer, its possession is already demonstrated. A man being offered a certificate is holding the thing the certificate would certify.

div.title: Verses 6-9: Abraham and the Nations

div.p: Just as Abraham "believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness" — know then that those of faith, these are sons of Abraham. And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: "In you shall all the nations be blessed." So then those of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

p.hi: Verse 6: "Just as Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.'"

div.p: The citation is Genesis 15:6, quoted in the Greek form: episteusen Abraam tō theō kai elogisthē autō eis dikaiosynēn.

Logizomai is a bookkeeping word: to reckon, to enter in an account, to credit. It belongs to commerce and administration before it belongs to theology, and its use here means that something was entered on Abraham's side of a ledger.
The position of this verse in Abraham's story is the argument. This has to be stated clearly because the whole strategy depends on it.

Genesis 15 is the chapter in which God brings Abram outside, shows him the stars, promises him offspring beyond counting, and Abram believes. Genesis 17 is the chapter, two chapters and (by the narrative's own reckoning) some thirteen years later, in which circumcision is instituted as the covenant sign for Abraham and his descendants.

If the teachers in Galatia were arguing from Genesis 17 — this is Abraham's covenant sign, therefore those who would join Abraham's family must receive it — then Paul's answer is to go to Genesis 15 and point out that the man was reckoned righteous before the sign existed. Whatever made Abraham right with God, it was not the thing the Galatians are being urged to undergo, because Abraham did not yet have it.
Paul makes this argument at greater length at Romans 4:9-12, where he draws the timing out explicitly. Here he simply cites the verse and lets its place in the narrative do the work.

p.hi: Verse 7: "Know then that those of faith, these are sons of Abraham."

div.p: Hoi ek pisteōs ("those out of faith") is a new construction, formed on a pattern the letter uses to name groups by what characterizes them: hoi ek peritomēs ("those of the circumcision," 2:12), hoi ex ergōn nomou ("those of works of law," 3:10). The preposition ek indicates source or origin — people whose defining derivation is faith.
Houtoi huioi eisin Abraam ("these are sons of Abraham"). The demonstrative is emphatic: these are the ones.

Descent from Abraham is the contested category in this entire dispute, and the claim being made is not that faith provides a substitute family for those who cannot have the real one. It is that faith identifies who the real family is.

p.hi: Verse 8: "And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.'"

div.p: Two features of this verse are remarkable, and both are easy to read past.

First, scripture is the subject of two active verbs. Hē graphē ("the scripture") foresaw (proidousa) and preached the gospel beforehand (proeuēngelisato). Scripture is personified as an agent that anticipated the present situation. The same personification recurs at 3:22 ("the scripture shut up everything under sin").

Second, the promise to Abraham is called the gospel. Proeuangelizomai ("to announce good news in advance") occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and Paul appears to have formed it for this sentence. The claim it makes is substantial: what Paul preaches to Gentiles is not a new message that has arrived to supplement an older arrangement. It is the message God announced to Abraham, arriving on time.

The citation conflates Genesis 12:3 ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed") with Genesis 18:18 ("all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him"), taking "all the nations" from the latter. The word is panta ta ethnē — the same word rendered "Gentiles" throughout this letter. In its own terms, without any interpretive pressure, the promise to Abraham was about the nations.

This is the positive engine of the whole argument, and it is often overshadowed by the negative material about law and curse that follows. Paul is not arguing that Gentiles may be admitted to something that was not designed for them. He is arguing that the arrangement was aimed at them from its first announcement.

p.hi: Verse 9: "So then those of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith."

div.p: Syn tō pistō Abraam ("with faithful Abraham"). The adjective pistos means both "believing" and "faithful," and here it names Abraham by the quality the citation attributed to him.
The preposition syn ("with, together with") is precise: the blessing is shared with Abraham, not transferred from him to someone else. Nobody is displaced.

What has been established by verse 9, before the difficult material begins. Abraham was reckoned righteous by believing, before circumcision existed. The promise made to him named the nations as its beneficiaries. Those characterized by faith are his sons and share his blessing. Every category that will govern the rest of the chapter — promise, blessing, offspring, inheritance — is Abrahamic, and all of them are in place before the law has been mentioned once.

div.title: Verses 10-14: Curse and Blessing

div.p: For as many as are of works of law are under a curse; for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, to do them." Now that no one is justified before God by law is evident, because "the righteous shall live by faith." But the law is not of faith; rather, "the one who does them shall live by them." Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us — for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" — so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

p.hi: Verse 10: "For as many as are of works of law are under a curse; for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, to do them.'"

div.p: The citation and its adjustments. The source is Deuteronomy 27:26, and Paul's wording matches neither the Hebrew nor the standard Greek exactly.
The Hebrew reads: "Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them."
The Greek version adds "all": "Cursed is every person who does not continue in all the words of this law to do them."

Paul writes: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, to do them." The phrase "the book of the law" is not in Deuteronomy 27:26; it is drawn from elsewhere in the same book (28:58, 61; 29:20-21; 30:10), where it designates the written covenant document as a whole.

The context of the verse he is quoting matters as much as its wording. Deuteronomy 27-30 is the covenant-sanctions section of the book. Chapter 27 stages a ceremony at Gerizim and Ebal in which the tribes pronounce a series of curses, and 27:26 is the last of them, summarizing the rest. Chapter 28 sets out the blessings for covenant faithfulness and then, at much greater length, the curses for covenant infidelity, culminating in defeat, deportation and exile. Chapters 29-30 look past the exile to a restoration.
So the sentence Paul quotes is not a general observation about human capability. It is the summary curse of a covenant document, in a section about what happens to the nation if it is unfaithful.

p.hi: The verse's logic has a gap, and how one fills it determines much of the letter.

div.p: Paul states a conclusion — those of works of law are under a curse — and supports it with a citation — cursed is everyone who does not do all. Getting from the citation to the conclusion requires a middle term, and Paul does not supply one. Three candidates have been proposed, and the evidence for each should be stated.

First: nobody does all of it. On this reading the unstated premise is that comprehensive obedience is not achievable, so everyone in the category is under the curse. This has been the dominant reading in Western Christianity since the sixteenth century.

The evidence bearing against it should be given its weight. Deuteronomy 30:11-14, three chapters after the verse Paul quotes and in the same covenant-sanctions block, says the opposite in as many words: "this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'... But the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it." Philippians 3:6 has Paul say of his own past that "as to righteousness under the law" he was blameless — he does not describe a man who tried and failed. Luke 1:6 describes Zechariah and Elizabeth as "righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord." And the Torah itself contains an elaborate provision for atonement — the sin offering, the guilt offering, the Day of Atonement — which presupposes failure and supplies its remedy. A covenant that builds in a remedy for failure is not a pass-or-fail examination, and treating unmet perfection as the covenant's implicit standard requires setting the remedy aside.

Second: the curse is the covenant's outstanding sanction. On this reading Paul's point is corporate and historical rather than individual and psychological. The curses of Deuteronomy 27-30 fell; the exile happened; and in the view of many Jews of this period the restoration promised in Deuteronomy 30 and the prophets had not yet fully arrived (Nehemiah 9:36, after the return: "behold, we are slaves this day"). To take on the covenant's badge now is therefore to enter under a judgment that is still in force rather than into a blessing.

Supporting evidence: the passage cited is a covenant-sanctions text, not a statement about human capacity; and verses 13-14 will describe a curse being lifted from one group ("us") so that a blessing may reach another ("the Gentiles"), which fits a specific covenantal curse better than a universal human condition.

Third: the emphasis falls on the doing. The citation ends tou poiēsai auta, "to do them," and on this reading the curse rests on those who take on the law's obligations without the corresponding life. Paul's target would then be the specific proposal in Galatia: adopting the marker without the substance.
Supporting evidence: 5:3, "he is a debtor to do the whole law," and 6:13, "not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves" — both of which press exactly this point.

The verse does not name its own premise, but the three candidates are not equally placed. The second and third are supported from within the letter and from the passage Paul is quoting. The first is supported chiefly by its long dominance, and it has to be held against Deuteronomy 30:11-14 in the same covenant block, against Paul's own description of himself at Philippians 3:6, against Luke 1:6, and against the existence of the atonement provisions. That is a burden the other two do not carry.
A reader should notice which premise a given interpretation has assumed — and should notice that the most familiar one is the one with the most to answer for.

p.hi: Verse 11: "Now that no one is justified before God by law is evident, because 'the righteous shall live by faith.'"

div.p: The citation is Habakkuk 2:4, and here too Paul has modified what he found.
The Greek version reads ho de dikaios ek pisteōs mou zēsetai — "the righteous shall live by my faithfulness," where the pronoun refers to God: the righteous person lives by God's reliability.
The Hebrew reads "the righteous shall live by his faithfulness" (be'emunato) — referring to the righteous person's own steadfastness.
Paul writes ho dikaios ek pisteōs zēsetai — dropping the pronoun entirely.

That is a deliberate act. He had two versions in front of him, each of which resolved the question one way, and he quoted it in a form that resolves it neither way. This bears directly on the pistis Christou question raised at 2:16: at the one place where Paul cites a text about faith and could have specified whose, he removed the specification.

It is worth adding what the underlying Hebrew word carries. Emunah comes from a root meaning firmness or reliability (the same root as "amen"). It denotes both trusting and being trustworthy, and Hebrew does not divide the two. The question "whose faith, and is it trust or fidelity?" may be a question the source text does not recognize.

p.hi: Verse 12: "But the law is not of faith; rather, 'the one who does them shall live by them.'"

div.p: The citation is Leviticus 18:5, quoted almost exactly.

Paul is setting two scriptural statements about living against each other: Habakkuk, where the righteous live by faith; Leviticus, where the one who does them lives by them. The contrast is between two operating principles, and it is worth being precise about what the contrast does and does not assert.
It does not assert that the law is bad, or that Leviticus 18:5 is untrue. Paul quotes it as scripture, without qualification.
It asserts that the two work differently, and that they are not the same principle.

What "life" means in Leviticus 18:5 is worth setting out, because much depends on it and the verse is regularly read at a higher pitch than its own context supports. The chapter is a body of legislation given to a people about to enter a land, and the verse stands at its head: "You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them." Deuteronomy states the same alternative in the same register: "I have set before you today life and good, death and evil... choose life, that you and your offspring may live, loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days, that you may dwell in the land" (Deuteronomy 30:15-20). The life on offer in these texts is life in the land, under blessing, in the presence of God — long life, flourishing, continuance as a people.

Whether that horizon extends to resurrection and the age to come is a question the verse does not raise. Paul cites it here for one purpose: to mark the law's operating principle as a different principle from the one Habakkuk names.

p.hi: Verse 13: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us — for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.'"

div.p: Exēgorasen ("redeemed") is a commercial word. Agorazō is "to buy in the marketplace" (the agora), and the prefix ex- adds "out of" — to buy something out of a condition, to purchase and remove. The word was used of buying a slave out of slavery. The same verb appears at 4:5, where Christ redeems "those under law."
The related word-group in the Greek scriptures is the exodus vocabulary: God "redeemed you from the house of slavery" (Deuteronomy 7:8; 9:26; 13:5; 15:15).
What they are bought out of is stated precisely: ek tēs kataras tou nomou, "from the curse of the law" — the specific curse named in verse 10, not a curse in general.
The citation, and Paul's two changes to it. The source is Deuteronomy 21:23.
The Greek version reads: kekatēramenos hypo theou pas kremamenos epi xylou — "cursed by God is everyone hanged on a tree."
Paul writes: epikataratos pas ho kremamenos epi xylou.

Change one: the word for "cursed." He replaces kekatēramenos with epikataratos — which is the exact word he used three verses earlier in the Deuteronomy 27:26 citation. After the substitution the two curses are named by the same term. The effect is to weld them: the thing Christ becomes in verse 13 is verbally identical to the thing the covenant pronounces in verse 10.
Change two: he drops "by God." The Greek version says God curses the hanged man. Paul omits it. The law's verdict is left standing as the agent, and the sentence does not say that God cursed him.

On applying Deuteronomy 21:23 to crucifixion. A reader may object that the passage does not describe crucifixion at all, and the objection is worth taking seriously. In Deuteronomy the sequence is: a man commits a capital crime, is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public display; the law's concern is that the body be taken down and buried the same day, "for a hanged man is cursed by God." The hanging is exposure after death, not the means of death. Crucifixion reverses that: the hanging is what kills.
But the application of the statute to crucifixion had already been made in Judea before Paul wrote, and it was a legal extension rather than a poetic association.

list.item: The Temple Scroll from Qumran (11Q19, column 64) legislates for the traitor and the informer: "you shall hang him on the tree and he shall die" — making the hanging the mode of execution — and then quotes Deuteronomy 21:22-23 over the ruling.
The Nahum commentary from Qumran (4Q169) describes "the Lion of Wrath... who hangs men alive on the tree," referring to a ruler's crucifixion of his opponents.
John 19:31 records that the bodies were taken down before sunset because of the approaching sabbath — which is Deuteronomy 21:23's same-day burial requirement being observed over crucified men.

The early preaching in Acts consistently calls the cross xylon, "tree" or "wood" (Acts 5:30; 10:39; 13:29), as does 1 Peter 2:24 — a word choice that only earns its keep if Deuteronomy 21:23 is in view.

div.p: So in Paul's setting the statute was already understood to reach crucifixion. The identification is a recognized halakhic extension, not a figure of speech, even though the procedure Deuteronomy describes is not the procedure Rome used.

p.hi: Verse 14: "So that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith."

div.p: Two purpose clauses, and the pronouns move between them. This movement is easy to miss and it matters.
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law" (v. 13)
→ "so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles"
→ "so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit."

Note what the middle clause does not say. It does not say "so that the Gentiles might be redeemed from the curse of the law." What arrives among the nations is the blessing of Abraham — which is the older promise of verse 8, made before Sinai and directed at the nations from its first announcement.

So two things are named in one sentence: a redemption from the law's curse, and the arrival of the Abrahamic blessing among the Gentiles, the second following from the first as its purpose. A reading of the letter has to say how these two are related, and the pronoun seam is where the question is posed.

"The promise of the Spirit" (tēn epangelian tou pneumatos) identifies what the Galatians already possess (3:2-5) as the promised thing itself. The argument has come full circle: the Spirit they can attest is the inheritance in question.

div.title: Verses 15-18: A Ratified Will

div.p: Brothers, I speak in human terms: even with a man's covenant, once it has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a codicil to it. Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say "and to offsprings," as of many, but as of one: "and to your offspring," who is Christ. This is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to void the promise. For if the inheritance is by law, it is no longer by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by promise.

p.hi: Verse 15: "Brothers, I speak in human terms: even with a man's covenant, once it has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a codicil to it."

div.p: Kata anthrōpon legō ("I speak according to man") signals an argument from ordinary human practice rather than from revelation.

Diathēkē is the pivot word of this paragraph, and it has two lives. In ordinary Greek usage of this period, a diathēkē is a will — a testamentary disposition of an estate, drawn up by one party, taking effect on defined terms. In the Greek scriptures, however, diathēkē is the standard rendering of the Hebrew berit, "covenant" — the term for God's arrangements with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and David.

Paul exploits both senses at once. The analogy works because a will, once executed, cannot be modified by outside parties. The application works because diathēkē is the word for what God made with Abraham.
Kekyrōmenēn ("ratified") is the perfect passive of kyroō, "to confirm, to validate, to make authoritative" — a legal term for an instrument that has taken effect.

Two things cannot be done to such an instrument: oudeis athetei ("no one annuls it") or epidiatassetai ("adds to it"). The second verb is precise: epi-diatassomai is to make an additional disposition — what a will's codicil does. Nobody can bolt a new clause onto a document already in force.

p.hi: Verse 16: "Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say 'and to offsprings,' as of many, but as of one: 'and to your offspring,' who is Christ."

div.p: The promise formula tō spermati sou ("to your offspring") appears at Genesis 13:15, 17:8 and 24:7.

This argument requires honest handling, because it has a well-known difficulty. Paul's point rests on the singular form of sperma. The difficulty is that sperma in Greek, like zera' in Hebrew, is a collective singular: the singular form regularly denotes a whole body of descendants, and Genesis uses it that way constantly — "I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted" (Genesis 13:16), where the singular noun plainly means a countless multitude. English "offspring" behaves the same way.
Paul knows this, and demonstrates that he knows it thirteen verses later: at 3:29 he writes "you are Abraham's sperma" of a whole community. He is not confused about Greek grammar.

What is happening, then, is not a claim about what the grammar compels but a reading of a kind attested in Jewish interpretation of the period, in which the form of a word in scripture is taken to carry significance. And what the reading establishes is a structure rather than a grammatical fact: the promise runs through one, and others enter it by belonging to him. That is exactly the structure 3:29 states — "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring." The singular is the hinge on which the many are attached.

p.hi: Verse 17: "This is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to void the promise."

div.p: Meta tetrakosia kai triakonta etē ("after 430 years") follows the Greek version of Exodus 12:40, which counts 430 years for the sojourn in Egypt and Canaan together; the Hebrew of that verse counts 430 years in Egypt alone. Paul is using the figure that measures from the patriarchs to the exodus, which is what his argument needs.
Ou akyroi ("does not invalidate") is the negated form of kyroō from verse 15 — the instrument was made valid, and the later arrangement does not un-validate it.

p.hi: Verse 18: "For if the inheritance is by law, it is no longer by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by promise."

div.p: Klēronomia ("inheritance") enters here and becomes the chapter's closing term at 3:29. In the Greek scriptures it is the word for Israel's allotted portion of the land (Deuteronomy 4:21, 38; 15:4; Joshua 11:23) and also, in the other direction, for Israel as God's own portion (Deuteronomy 9:26, 29; 32:9). The word carries the idea of something received because of who one is, not something earned.
The disjunction ei... ouketi ("if... then no longer") sets law and promise as alternative bases for one and the same inheritance.

It is worth being exact about what this argument claims and what it does not. It does not claim that the promise is a superior kind of thing to the covenant at Sinai. It claims that the two are different instruments with different logics, that the promise was ratified first, and that a later instrument cannot rewrite an earlier one that is already in force. The operative words in verse 17 are ou akyroi — it does not invalidate. Priority and irrevocability are the terms of the argument, not rank.

The distinction matters. An argument from rank invites the conclusion that the lesser thing may be retired. An argument from priority does not: it leaves the later instrument standing and simply denies that it can overwrite the earlier one.

div.title: Verses 19-22: Why Then the Law?

div.p: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one. Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that was able to make alive, then righteousness would indeed have been by law. But the scripture shut up everything under sin, so that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

p.hi: Verse 19a: "Why then the law?"

div.p: Ti oun ho nomos is the question the preceding argument forces. If the promise came first and cannot be added to, and if the inheritance runs on promise rather than law, then Sinai needs accounting for. The question is an objection Paul raises against himself, and the answer occupies the rest of the chapter.

p.hi: Verse 19b: "It was added because of transgressions."

div.p: Prosetethē ("it was added") is the first part of the answer and it is a word about relation. The law is an addition to something already standing — the promise of verses 15-18. It is not a replacement for it, not an independent arrangement, and not the thing the promise was leading up to. Whatever else follows, the letter's own term for how Sinai relates to the Abrahamic promise is "added."
Tōn parabaseōn charin ("because of transgressions") is ambiguous. The preposition charin with the genitive means "for the sake of, on account of, with a view to," and three readings are available:
To restrain them. The law was added to hold transgression in check — a curb.

To produce or expose them. The law was added so that wrongdoing would be identified as transgression. This is the line Paul takes elsewhere: "where there is no law, neither is there transgression" (Romans 4:15); "the law came in that the trespass might increase" (Romans 5:20); and the extended argument of Romans 7:7-13.
To deal with them. The law was added because transgression existed and a system for handling it was needed — which is what the sacrificial and purity legislation supplies.

The noun itself is worth noting. Parabasis is formed from parabainō, "to step across," and denotes crossing a line that has been drawn. It differs from hamartia, "missing the mark," in presupposing a boundary already marked out. A transgression requires a stated law to be transgressed, which is what makes the second reading grammatically natural even though the third fits the sacrificial system better.

p.hi: Verse 19c: "Until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made."

div.p: Achris hou elthē to sperma sets a terminus, and the question is what it terminates.

Grammatically, a temporal clause limits the clause it modifies. What is being limited here is the adding-because-of-transgressions — the function just described — rather than the law's existence. The letter maintains this pattern consistently: at 3:25 it does not say "the law is abolished" but "we are no longer under a paidagōgos." What ends, in every formulation Paul uses, is a relation to the law rather than the law itself.
Whether that distinction bears the weight some readers place on it is a fair question, but the distinction is in the text and is not an interpreter's invention.

p.hi: Verse 19d: "Having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator."

div.p: Diatageis di' angelōn en cheiri mesitou.
The tradition that angels attended the giving of the law was widespread, and in most of its occurrences it is honorific. This should be known before the phrase is read as disparagement.

list.item: Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek version reads: "The LORD came from Sinai... at his right hand, angels with him." (The Hebrew is different and more obscure; the Greek supplies the angels.)
Acts 7:53, in Stephen's speech, has Israel "receive the law by the ordinances of angels" — eis diatagas angelōn, from the same root as Paul's diatageis.
Hebrews 2:2 speaks of "the word spoken through angels."

Josephus puts into Herod's mouth the claim that the Jews "learned the noblest of our doctrines and the holiest of our laws through angels sent from God" (Antiquities 15.136) — and it is said as a boast.
Jubilees 1:27-2:1 has the angel of the presence dictate the law to Moses.

div.p: The presence of angels at Sinai was therefore, in most Jewish usage, part of the glory of the occasion, not a diminishment of it.

"By the hand of a mediator" (en cheiri mesitou) is a Semitic idiom for agency, and the mediator is Moses, who stood between God and the people at Sinai at their own request (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:5, "I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD").
Whether Paul is invoking the honorific tradition or turning it to a different purpose depends on how the next sentence is read.

p.hi: Verse 20: "Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one."

div.p: This is the most obscure sentence in the letter, and honesty requires saying so. Commentators have catalogued hundreds of proposed interpretations. The elements are: a mediator (mesitēs) implies more than one party; God is one.

The least strained reading takes it as an argument about directness. A mediated arrangement requires two parties and an intermediary between them. The promise to Abraham had no such structure: God spoke, and there was no second contracting party and no go-between. On this reading verse 20 continues the argument of 15-18 — a unilateral instrument cannot be overturned by a later bilateral one.

Other proposals have taken the "one" to be the single offspring of verse 16; or read it as a denial of the law's divine origin; or as an affirmation that the one God stands behind both arrangements, so that no conflict can arise between them.

The sentence does not decide among these, and it should not be made to carry weight its obscurity cannot bear. Whatever else is true, "God is one" is the opening line of Israel's daily confession (Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema), and Paul is asserting something about God's unity in the middle of an argument about two arrangements. Beyond that, caution is warranted.

p.hi: Verse 21: "Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that was able to make alive, then righteousness would indeed have been by law."

div.p: The question ho nomos kata tōn epangeliōn tou theou ("is the law against the promises of God?") is the one everything since verse 19 invites. Paul rejects it with mē genoito, his strongest negation.

p.hi: The reason he gives is the clearest statement in the letter about what the law was and was not for, and it should be read exactly.

div.p: Ei gar edothē nomos ho dynamenos zōopoiēsai, ontōs ek nomou an ēn hē dikaiosynē — "if a law had been given that was able to make alive, righteousness would indeed have been by law."

The verb. Zōopoieō is "to make alive, to give life," and its use elsewhere is resurrection language: God "gives life to the dead" (Romans 4:17); "he will also give life to your mortal bodies" (Romans 8:11); "in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22, and again at 15:36, 45).
The grammar. This is a contrary-to-fact conditional — the construction used for a condition known to be untrue. No such law was given.

What it therefore asserts. The law is not opposed to the promise, because it was never issued to do the promise's work. It was not a failed attempt at giving life; it was not an attempt at all. This is a statement about the law's remit, not about human performance under it.

The distinction is worth pressing, because the two are easily conflated. "A law was given that could make alive, but nobody managed to keep it" is a different proposition from "no law able to make alive was given." Paul writes the second. And he writes it as the defence of the law against the charge of standing against God's promises — which means that on his own account, the law's inability to give life is not a deficiency in it but a fact about what it was for.

p.hi: Verse 22: "But the scripture shut up everything under sin, so that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe."

div.p: Synekleisen ("shut up together, enclosed, confined") is used in the Greek scriptures of shutting someone into a place from which they cannot get out — "you have not shut me up into the hand of the enemy" (Psalm 31:8, LXX 30:9); of the men of Keilah shutting David in (1 Samuel 23:11-12).
The subject is hē graphē, "the scripture," personified as at verse 8.
Ta panta is neuter plural, "all things" — broader than "all people." The confinement is comprehensive rather than a statement about individuals.
The purpose is stated: hina hē epangelia ek pisteōs Iēsou Christou dothē tois pisteuousin. The same ambiguous genitive from 2:16 recurs; the same options apply.

div.title: Verses 23-25: The Escort

div.p: But before faith came, we were kept in custody under law, confined until the coming faith should be revealed. So that the law has become our paidagogos unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a paidagogos.

p.hi: Verse 23: "But before faith came, we were kept in custody under law, confined until the coming faith should be revealed."

div.p: Ephrouroumetha ("we were being guarded") is from phroureō, a military term: to garrison, to keep under guard, to post a watch. It is worth knowing that this verb does not settle its own connotation. Paul uses it at Philippians 4:7 in an unambiguously protective sense: "the peace of God... will guard (phrourēsei) your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus." A garrison may confine a prisoner or protect a city; the word alone does not say which.
It is paired here with synkleiomenoi, the participle of the verb from verse 22, which does suggest confinement.

Whether the custody in view is protective (Israel kept safe until the appointed time) or restrictive (Israel held under constraint) is therefore not settled by the vocabulary, and the choice colours everything that follows in the paragraph.

The temporal frame is notable: pro tou elthein tēn pistin ("before the faith came") and eis tēn mellousan pistin apokalyphthēnai ("until the faith about to be revealed"). "Faith" here appears with the article and functions almost as a period marker — an era that arrived at a point in time — rather than as an individual's act of believing. Something came; before it came, things were arranged one way.

p.hi: Verses 24-25: "So that the law has become our paidagogos unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a paidagogos."

div.p: What a paidagogos was. This needs setting out plainly, because the English "tutor," "schoolmaster" and "guardian" all mislead, and the image is doing the argument's work.

In a Greco-Roman household of any means, the paidagōgos was a slave — typically an older, trusted one — assigned to a boy from roughly the age of six until he came of age in his mid-teens. His job was custodial and disciplinary, not educational. He walked the boy to the schoolmaster and home again, carried his things, kept him out of trouble, supervised his manners, and administered correction. He was frequently depicted in ancient art with a staff or cane. He did not give the lessons; the didaskalos did that.
Two things follow, and both bear on the argument.
The paidagōgos was not the teacher. He was the escort who got the boy to the teacher.

His term ended at the boy's majority, and it ended by the calendar rather than by any failure on his part. Nothing about the paidagōgos being discharged implies he was bad at his job, or that the household repudiated him. The boy grew up. That is all.
Eis Christon ("unto Christ") can be read two ways and the choice matters.
Temporally: "until Christ." The paidagōgos's term ran until the Messiah came.

Purposively: "to lead us to Christ." The law's function was to bring people to Christ — and, in the traditional Protestant development of this reading, to do so by exposing sin and thereby driving a person to seek grace.

The evidence favours the temporal reading. Verse 25 says the paidagōgos's term has ended now that faith has come, which is a statement about time and not about pedagogy. The parallel with achris hou at 3:19 ("until the offspring should come") points the same way. And the household image itself resists the purposive reading: the escort did not teach the lesson or convince the boy of anything; he delivered him to the door.

Note also what verse 25 says and does not say. It does not say the law is abolished, or ended, or set aside. It says "we are no longer under a paidagōgos" — ouketi hypo paidagōgon esmen. What has ended is a position under a supervision.

The pronouns, and the problem they pose. Verses 23-25 are first person plural throughout: we were kept in custody; we are no longer under a paidagōgos. Verse 26 shifts abruptly to the second person: "for you are all sons of God."

The most natural reading of the shift is that "we" designates Jews and "you" the Galatian Gentile recipients — which would mean that the custody and its ending are stated of Jews, with Paul including himself. The alternative is that "we" is a rhetorical inclusive which Paul then narrows for emphasis.
The shift is real on any account, and any reading of the passage has to say what the ending of the paidagōgos's term consists of for the group Paul places himself in.

div.title: Verses 26-29: Sons, Offspring, and Heirs

div.p: For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise.

p.hi: Verse 26: "For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus."

div.p: Pantes gar huioi theou este. The pronoun becomes second person and pantes ("all") is emphatic.

Sonship of God is Israel's designation in the scriptures, and the reader should hear it as such rather than as a general religious idea. "Israel is my firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22). "You are the sons of the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1). "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1). "I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn" (Jeremiah 31:9). To tell Gentile congregations that they are all sons of God is to apply Israel's own family language to them.

p.hi: Verse 27: "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."

div.p: Christon enedysasthe ("you put on Christ"), from endyō, "to clothe, to put on a garment."

The clothing metaphor is well established in the Greek scriptures for being invested with a quality or condition: "he has clothed me with the garments of salvation" (Isaiah 61:10); "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me" (Job 29:14); "let your priests be clothed with righteousness" (Psalm 132:9); and, of God's own equipping, "he put on righteousness as a breastplate" (Isaiah 59:17). To put on Christ is to be invested with him — to appear, and to be dealt with, as what one now wears.
Baptism is named here as the point at which this incorporation occurred, without further elaboration. The letter does not develop it, and nothing in the argument turns on the mechanics.

p.hi: Verse 28: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus."

div.p: The three pairs, and the different construction of the third. The first two are joined by oude ("nor"): Ioudaios oude Hellēn; doulos oude eleutheros. The third uses kai ("and"): arsen kai thēly.

That change is not random. Arsen kai thēly is the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek version: arsen kai thēly epoiēsen autous, "male and female he made them." The third pair is quoted from the creation account, which points the formula back past Abraham, past Sinai, to the making of humanity.
What ouk eni denies. The verb eni is a shortened form of enestin, "there is in" — so the statement is that within the sphere named, en Christō Iēsou, these distinctions are not present.
The question is what kind of absence is meant, and the text requires care here.

The distinctions plainly continue to exist as facts. Paul goes on addressing slaves and free people, men and women, Jews and Greeks throughout his correspondence as the categories they are. This very letter's entire argument requires that Jews and Gentiles remain distinguishable — there would be nothing to dispute otherwise, and Paul describes himself as a Jew by birth at 2:15 without apology.

What the formula most naturally denies, then, is their bearing on standing within the sphere named: none of the three determines who is a son of God, who has put on Christ, who inherits. That is what the surrounding verses are about — 26 and 27 before it, 29 after it.

Whether more than that is intended — whether the formula also envisages the eventual dissolution of the distinctions themselves, or their preservation within a unity that does not rank them — the verse does not say. It says what does not obtain, and then it says something positive: pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christō Iēsou. And the "one" is heis, masculine singular: not "one thing," but one person. The community is described as a single individual.

p.hi: Verse 29: "And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise."

div.p: The chapter closes on the terms with which its scriptural argument began.

Sperma ("offspring") is the word from verse 16, now used collectively of a whole community — which is precisely the structure the singular argument was built to produce. The promise ran to one; the many belong to it by belonging to him. Verse 16 and verse 29 are the two halves of a single move, and neither works without the other.
