Alētheia ("truth") echoes 2:5 and 2:14, where Paul twice speaks of "the truth of the gospel" — once of a stand taken in Jerusalem and once of a line Peter failed to walk straight toward. The truth in view is not a general commitment to honesty but this specific message.

p.hi: Verse 8: "This persuasion is not from him who calls you."

div.p: Hē peismonē ("the persuasion, the persuading") occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is rare in Greek generally. It denotes the act or the effect of persuading — the campaign of argument being conducted among them. The word choice may be a play on the peithesthai of verse 7: a persuasion that keeps you from being persuaded by the truth.

Ek tou kalountos hymas ("from the one who calls you") uses the present participle: God is presently calling, which is a small but real note of hope in a hostile paragraph. The same participle appeared at 1:6, where the Galatians are "deserting him who called you." The preposition ek denies divine origin.

Whatever arguments the other teachers are making, and whatever scriptures they are citing — and they were surely citing scripture, since Genesis 17 is on their side of the question — the campaign does not come from the God who called these congregations.

p.hi: Verse 9: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump."

div.p: A proverb. Paul uses the identical sentence at 1 Corinthians 5:6, in a quite different context.

Zymē is leaven — in practice a piece of fermented dough kept back from a previous batch and worked into a new one to start it rising. The point of the proverb is disproportion: a very small quantity transforms the entire mass, and once it is in, it cannot be confined to the part it started in.

In Israel's scriptures leaven carries a further association. All leaven was to be removed from the house at Passover (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7), and leaven was excluded from offerings burnt on the altar (Leviticus 2:11). From that it came to serve as an image of a permeating and corrupting influence — as in "beware the leaven of the Pharisees" (Mark 8:15).
The application here is to containment. The Galatians may suppose that accepting one requirement leaves the rest of what they have intact. The proverb denies that such a thing is possible.

p.hi: Verse 10: "I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view; and the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he is."

div.p: Egō pepoitha eis hymas en kyriō. The perfect pepoitha ("I have been persuaded, and so am confident") describes a settled state rather than a momentary feeling. The basis is stated as en kyriō, "in the Lord": Paul's confidence is not in these congregations' resilience but is located outside them.

This is the most hopeful sentence in the letter, and it sits between the severance of verse 4 and the bitterness of verse 12. Both belong to the same man writing the same paragraph, and a reading that keeps only one of the two registers has lost the letter's actual temperature.
Ouden allo phronēsete ("you will think nothing otherwise") uses phroneō, "to have a mindset, to be disposed, to take a view." It is a verb about settled disposition rather than momentary opinion.

Ho tarassōn hymas ("the one troubling you") is singular, whereas 1:7 had a plural ("some who are troubling you"). Whether a single ringleader is in view or the singular is generalizing cannot be determined, though the closing phrase suggests the latter.

Bastasei to krima ("he will bear the judgment") uses bastazō — the verb that appears at Acts 15:10 for bearing a yoke, and that will appear three times in the next chapter, of burdens (6:2), of a load (6:5), and of Paul's own scars (6:17).

Hostis ean ē ("whoever he may be") is striking and should not be passed over. Paul declines to make the man's identity relevant — which is precisely the principle established at 1:8-9, where even Paul himself or an angel from heaven would fall under the curse for preaching another gospel. The messenger's credentials are not the test, and Paul applies the rule to his opponents exactly as he applied it to himself.

p.hi: Verse 11: "But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed."

div.p: The verse presupposes an accusation: someone has said that Paul preaches circumcision. What lay behind such a claim the letter does not say, and speculation is not required. The word eti ("still") implies a contrast with an earlier period — perhaps his life before the call, perhaps something else.

The argument is a proof by contradiction, and it runs on a fact Paul takes as public and undeniable: he is being persecuted. Diōkomai is present passive — an ongoing condition, not a past episode. If he were preaching what the other teachers preach, that would stop, because their programme is precisely what removes the offence.
Ara katērgētai to skandalon tou staurou ("then the stumbling-block of the cross has been abolished"). Katargeō is the verb of 5:4, here in the perfect.

Skandalon originally denoted the trigger-stick of a trap — the piece that springs when an animal touches it — and by extension anything that causes a person to stumble and fall. The Greek scriptures use it for an obstacle placed in someone's path: "you shall not put a stumbling block (skandalon) before the blind" (Leviticus 19:14).

p.hi: What makes the cross offensive is worth stating, since the sentence assumes it and a modern reader does not feel it.

div.p: Crucifixion was a Roman method of public execution reserved for slaves, rebels and provincials without citizenship. The condemned man was fixed to a beam and left in the open to die slowly, in view of passers-by, and often left unburied. It was designed to humiliate as much as to kill, and Roman writers of the period treat it as a subject barely fit for polite mention. Cicero calls the very word unfit for a Roman citizen's ears.

To claim that God's decisive act took that form was not merely surprising; it was disgraceful. Paul says as much elsewhere: the crucified Messiah is "a stumbling block (skandalon) to Jews and folly to Gentiles" (1 Corinthians 1:23).

And the offence increases if the cross is claimed to be sufficient on its own, because that empties the recognized route of entry of its significance. Supplement the cross with circumcision and the offence subsides — the message becomes a variant of something already intelligible — and the persecution subsides with it.

This verse and 6:12 form a matched pair: Paul argues from his own persecution that he cannot be preaching circumcision, and argues that his opponents press it precisely in order to avoid what he suffers.

p.hi: Verse 12: "I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!"
Ophelon kai apokopsontai hoi anastatountes hymas.

div.p: Ophelon expresses an unattainable wish — "would that," "if only." Apokoptō is "to cut off, to amputate," and in the middle voice with no stated object it was the standard term for castration.

p.hi: Two contexts sharpen the sentence, and both should be known before it is dismissed as mere abuse.

div.p: The Torah's own ruling. Deuteronomy 23:1 in the Greek version excludes from the assembly of the LORD the man "whose testicles are crushed or whose male organ is cut off" — apokekommenos, the same verb. So the wish carries a legal edge: men who are pressing an entrance requirement on others would, by taking their own logic one step further, disqualify themselves from the assembly under the very law they champion. Paul is not simply being crude; he is making an argument about where the logic of cutting flesh for standing terminates.

The local religious landscape. The region of Galatia was strongly associated with the cult of Cybele, the Great Mother, whose priests — the galli — were self-castrated, a practice notorious throughout the Mediterranean world. A congregation in that region would not need it explained. The wish therefore also says: follow this reasoning to its end and you arrive where the pagan priests already are — which is the same move the letter made at 4:8-10, where taking on the programme is described as a return to what they came out of.

Hoi anastatountes hymas ("those who unsettle you") is the third designation for the other teachers, after "those troubling you" (1:7) and "the one troubling you" (5:10). Anastatoō means "to stir up, to turn upside down, to throw into disorder"; Acts uses it of those who "turned the world upside down" (17:6) and of an insurrectionist (21:38). The word is about public disturbance rather than private error.

div.title: Verses 13-15: Freedom for Service

div.p: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

p.hi: Verse 13: "For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another."

div.p: The letter turns here. Everything to this point has argued that the Galatians must not do something; from here Paul says what they should do. It is worth noticing that the turn does not come with a new premise — it comes with the same word the previous section ended on.

Ep' eleutheria eklēthēte ("you were called to freedom"). The passive verb has God as its implied agent, as at 1:6 and 5:8. Freedom is not something they achieved or claimed; it is what they were summoned into.

Aphormēn tē sarki ("an opportunity for the flesh"). Aphormē is a military term: the base of operations, the fortified position from which a campaign is launched, the starting-point of an expedition. Paul uses it several times for a pretext or an opening someone exploits (Romans 7:8, 11; 2 Corinthians 5:12; 11:12).

The warning is therefore not that freedom might be misunderstood but that it might be used — that it could become the staging ground from which something else operates. A base of operations is where a campaign begins.
Dia tēs agapēs douleuete allēlois ("through love serve one another as slaves").

The verb is the paradox, and it is unmistakable in Greek. Douleuō is the verb of slavery — from doulos, "slave." It is the same root as the douleia in "yoke of slavery" twelve verses earlier, the same root as the enslavement under the stoicheia at 4:3 and 4:8-9, and the same root as the katadoulōsousin ("that they might enslave us") of 2:4.
Paul has spent the letter arguing that his readers must not be enslaved. He now commands them to be slaves to each other.

The point is not verbal cleverness. Freedom in this letter is not the absence of obligation; it is the transfer of it. What Christ ended was a servitude imposed as the price of standing. What replaces it is a servitude freely given to people who are in no position to demand it. The Galatians are not being released from service into autonomy, and any account of the letter's "freedom" that omits verse 13 has taken half a sentence.

p.hi: Verse 14: "For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'"

div.p: Ho gar pas nomos en heni logō peplērōtai. Two things in this clause require attention, and they are the chapter's central data.
*First, the verb, and its difference from 5:3.*

Peplērōtai is the perfect passive of plēroō — "to fill, to fill up, to bring to completion, to fulfil." The perfect tense in Greek describes a completed action whose result stands: not "is being fulfilled," not "will be fulfilled," but "stands fulfilled."

Eleven verses earlier, Paul said the man who accepts circumcision is a debtor holon ton nomon poiēsai — "to do the whole law." Here he says ho pas nomos... peplērōtai — the whole law stands fulfilled in one word.

Two different verbs, two different constructions, both applied to "the whole law," within eleven verses of each other. Whatever Paul is doing, he is not saying the same thing twice, and the difference between doing and fulfilling is where the chapter's problem lives.
*Second, the move itself is a recognized Jewish one, and this is decisive for how it should be heard.*
Summarizing the Torah in a single principle was a familiar exercise, and in none of its known instances did it mean that the remainder could be discarded.

Hillel, a generation before Paul, asked by a Gentile to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, answered: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary — go and learn" (b. Shabbat 31a). The summary is immediately followed by an instruction to go and study everything it summarizes. Nobody hearing it would have taken it as permission to skip the rest.

Jesus, asked for the greatest commandment, names love of God and love of neighbour and adds: "On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets" (Matthew 22:37-40). The verb is kremannymi, "to hang," as a door hangs on its hinge. A hinge does not replace the door; it is what the door depends on and turns on, and a door with no hinge does not open.

Micah 6:8 performs the same reduction from within the prophets: "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?"

Paul himself does it again at Romans 13:8-10, and there he makes the relation explicit: he lists four commandments from the Decalogue, says they "are summed up in this word, 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself,'" and concludes "love is therefore the plērōma of the law" — the fullness, that which fills it up.

The citation is Leviticus 19:18, quoted from the Greek version. It is worth noticing where it stands in its own book: in the middle of a chapter of Torah legislation, surrounded by commandments about leaving gleanings for the poor, paying wages on time, not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind, judging without partiality, and not bearing a grudge. Paul is quoting Torah, as Torah, as the summary of Torah.

p.hi: Verse 15: "But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another."

div.p: Daknete kai katesthiete ("you bite and eat up"). Both verbs belong to the animal world. Daknō is what a dog or a snake does. Katesthiō is devouring, eating something down — the verb used of birds eating the seed in the parable of the sower.
Analōthēte ("you be consumed") is from analiskō, "to use up completely, to spend, to destroy." It is the word for consuming a resource until nothing remains.

This verse changes how the rest of the chapter should be read, and it is easy to skip past. It indicates that the crisis in Galatia had already produced conflict inside the congregations — not merely a theological disagreement between Paul and some visitors, but people tearing at each other. The catalogue of vices at 5:19-21 and the closing warning at 5:26 should both be read with this in view.

div.title: Verses 16-18: Spirit and Flesh

div.p: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing what you want. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law.

p.hi: Verse 16: "But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh."

div.p: Pneumati peripateite ("walk by the Spirit"). Peripateō is "to walk about," and its use for the conduct of life is a Jewish idiom rather than a Greek one. It renders the Hebrew halakh, "to walk," which is the standard scriptural way of speaking about how a person lives: "blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked" (Psalm 1:1); "teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth" (Psalm 86:11); "he has told you... what the LORD requires of you: to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). The noun halakhah, the body of practical rulings on how to live, comes from the same root.
To speak of walking is therefore to speak of daily conduct, step by step, and not of a stance or a state.

Epithymian sarkos ou mē telesēte uses ou mē with the subjunctive — the strongest form of negation available in Greek, a categorical denial about the future. Teleō is "to bring to completion, to carry out, to accomplish."

The construction is a promise attached to a command rather than two commands. Paul does not say "walk by the Spirit and resist the flesh," which would give the reader two things to do. He gives one thing to do and states what will follow from it.

p.hi: Verse 17: "For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing what you want."

div.p: Hē gar sarx epithymei kata tou pneumatos, to de pneuma kata tēs sarkos. The verb epithymeō ("to desire, to set the heart on") governs both clauses, which puts flesh and Spirit in the same grammatical position: both want something, and each wants against the other.

Antikeitai allēlois ("they lie opposed to one another") describes a standing structural opposition rather than an occasional friction. Antikeimai is used of adversaries in a lawsuit and of opposing armies drawn up against each other.
The final clause is genuinely ambiguous and should be reported as such rather than resolved by translation. Hina mē ha ean thelēte tauta poiēte — "so that you may not do the things you want."
Whose wanting is being frustrated, and which things? Three readings:

list.item: The flesh prevents the good one wills. This is the reading that assimilates the verse to Romans 7 ("I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate").
The Spirit prevents the evil one wills. This fits the promise of verse 16, where the Spirit's leading is what makes the flesh's desire uncompleted.
The conflict as such means one cannot simply act on unexamined desire. There is no neutral ground on which the will operates autonomously; a person is governed by one or the other.

div.p: The sentence does not specify, and its immediate context supports the second and third as much as the first: the paragraph is about being led by one power or the other, and it is framed by a promise rather than by a lament.

p.hi: Verse 18: "But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law."
Ei de pneumati agesthe, ouk este hypo nomon.

div.p: The phrase hypo nomon is the one fixed at 4:4-5, where Christ himself was "born under law" in order to redeem those under law. Since Christ observed Torah, the phrase cannot describe Torah practice; it denotes a standing under the law's jurisdiction and sanctions.

Agesthe ("you are being led") is present passive — an ongoing condition in which the Spirit is the active party. The verb is used of leading an animal, of conducting a person somewhere, of a defendant being brought before a court.

The verse's placement is what keeps it from being misread, and it should be noticed. It stands immediately before a catalogue of behaviours whose practitioners "will not inherit the kingdom of God" (5:21), and three verses before a list of what the Spirit produces. Whatever "not under law" means here, it is stated in a context wholly concerned with conduct, and it is followed at once by a severe warning about conduct.

So the sentence is not a release from moral obligation. Any reading that makes it one has to explain why Paul immediately supplies a list of things that forfeit the kingdom, and why he says three verses later that there is no law against what the Spirit grows.

div.title: Verses 19-21: The Works of the Flesh

div.p: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who practise such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

p.hi: Verse 19a: "Now the works of the flesh are evident."

div.p: Phanera ("evident, manifest, out in the open") declares that these are not hidden, disputed, or a matter for expert discernment. Nobody needs to be told that they belong on the list, which is why Paul can simply name them without argument.

Ta erga tēs sarkos ("the works of the flesh") uses erga, the plural noun that has run through the letter in the phrase erga nomou, "works of law" (2:16; 3:2, 5, 10). The choice of noun is deliberate and will contrast sharply with verse 22.
The list, and its shape. Fifteen items are named, and they fall into recognizable groups:
Sexual (three): porneia (sexual immorality of any kind — the general term), akatharsia (impurity, uncleanness), aselgeia (unrestrained indecency, behaviour that has stopped caring who sees).
Religious (two): eidōlolatria (idolatry — literally image-service), pharmakeia (the word covers drugs, potions, poisons and magic together, since the practices were not separated).

Social (eight): echthrai (enmities, hostilities), eris (strife, quarrelling), zēlos (jealousy — the same word that named Paul's own former zeal at 1:14, here in its destructive sense), thymoi (outbursts of rage, plural: not a temperament but episodes), eritheiai (rivalries, self-seeking, working for one's own advancement), dichostasiai (dissensions, standings-apart), haireseis (factions, parties — the word from which "heresy" descends, but here meaning a division of the community into camps), phthonoi (envyings).
Excess (two): methai (drunkenness), kōmoi (carousing, revels).

The distribution is worth counting, and it is the key to reading the list correctly. Eight of the fifteen — more than half — concern the breakdown of relations within a group. Given that verse 15 has just described the Galatians biting and devouring one another, and that verse 26 will close the chapter on provoking and envying one another, the weighting is not accidental.

This is not a general catalogue of vice dropped into the letter from a stock of such lists. It is aimed. A congregation that has fallen out with itself over a theological crisis is being shown what its own behaviour belongs to.
The closing phrase kai ta homoia toutois ("and things like these") marks the list as representative rather than complete.

p.hi: Verse 21b: "I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who practise such things will not inherit the kingdom of God."

div.p: Prolegō hymin kathōs proeipon ("I tell you in advance, as I told you before"). Both verbs carry the pro- prefix. This was part of Paul's original teaching among them, not a new threat produced by the present crisis — which means the Galatians have heard it and are behaving this way anyway.
Hoi ta toiauta prassontes ("those who practise such things") uses the present participle of prassō.

The tense is load-bearing and should not be flattened in translation. The present participle denotes continued or habitual action — a practice, a settled way of going on — rather than a single act. The sentence is not about a person who does one of these things once; it is about a person whose life consists in them. English "practise" catches this; "do" does not.

Basileian theou ou klēronomēsousin ("will not inherit the kingdom of God"). The verb is klēronomeō, from the inheritance word-group that has run through the letter: the inheritance of 3:18, the heirs of 3:29 and 4:7, the son who is an heir at 4:7. The warning is expressed as an inheritance not entered — the same grammar as 5:4 (a connection severed) and 6:8-9 (a harvest not reaped).

And the addressees are the same people addressed throughout: the Galatian believers, who received the Spirit (3:2), who are sons of God (3:26), who are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise (3:29), in whose hearts the Spirit cries Abba (4:6).

div.title: Verses 22-26: The Fruit of the Spirit

div.p: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law. And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in line by the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

p.hi: Verses 22-23a: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control."

div.p: Ho karpos tou pneumatos — and karpos is singular, against the plural erga of verse 19.
The contrast was available in the vocabulary and Paul took it. One word would have served for both lists; he used two, and the difference between them is not decorative.

Erga are things made — produced by effort, various, each one a separate accomplishment that can be counted and displayed. It is the noun that has appeared throughout the letter in "works of law," and it will appear again at 6:13 in the boasting the other teachers want to do.

Karpos is what grows — borne rather than manufactured, arising from what the plant is rather than from what it decides, and singular even when it hangs in many pieces on the same tree. A farmer does not achieve fruit; he tends a tree and the fruit follows from its nature.
Nine qualities are named as one crop:

Agapē (love), which was the content of 5:13-14 and will be the content of 6:2. Chara (joy). Eirēnē (peace — the word rendering shalom, wholeness rather than mere absence of conflict). Makrothymia (patience; literally "long-temperedness," the opposite of the thymoi, the short outbursts, in the vice list). Chrēstotēs (kindness, usefulness to others — the quality of being good for something). Agathōsynē (goodness). Pistis. Prautēs (gentleness — not weakness but strength under control; the word is used of a horse that has been broken, which has lost none of its power and gained a rider). Enkrateia (self-mastery, having power over oneself — notable as the last item, since it is precisely what the flesh's works lack).

Pistis in this list may be rendered "faith" or "faithfulness" — the same ambiguity that runs through 2:16 and 3:11, and a standing reminder that the Greek word does not divide the way the English pair does.

Two of the nine are direct answers to items in the vice list: makrothymia against thymoi, and enkrateia against the whole final group. And the first, agapē, is the answer to the eight social vices at once.

p.hi: Verse 23b: "Against such things there is no law."

div.p: Kata tōn toioutōn ouk estin nomos is grammatically ambiguous: tōn toioutōn may be neuter ("such things," the qualities just listed) or masculine ("such people," those who bear them). The Greek forms are identical and the sentence works either way.
Either way the substance is the same: the law does not stand against what the Spirit produces.

This is the clearest indication in the letter that the Spirit's work and the law's direction are not opposed to one another. There is no commandment that forbids love, or patience, or self-control; nothing in the Torah is transgressed by a person who is gentle. What the Spirit grows is not what the law prohibits.

Read together with 5:18 — "if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law" — the two verses give a coherent position that neither gives alone. A person led by the Spirit is not in the law's crosshairs, because what the Spirit produces is what the law was pointing toward. Neither verse says the law's content has been withdrawn, and the second explicitly says the opposite.

p.hi: Verse 24: "And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires."

div.p: Tēn sarka estaurōsan ("they crucified the flesh"). Two features are easy to miss and both matter.

The subject is the believers. Paul does not write "the flesh was crucified" or "God crucified the flesh." Hoi tou Christou Iēsou... estaurōsan — those who belong to Christ Jesus did it. The verb is active and they are its subject.
The tense is aorist — a completed action, viewed as a single whole rather than as a process.

Syn tois pathēmasin kai tais epithymiais ("with its passions and desires") specifies what went to the cross with it. Epithymia is the noun from the verb of 5:16-17, so the sentence closes what that passage opened.

The verb connects backward to 2:19-20 ("I have been crucified with Christ") and forward to 6:14 ("the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world"). Crucifixion is the letter's recurring image for a decisive and irreversible severance, and in every instance it involves participation in Christ's own death rather than a separate act performed alongside it.

p.hi: Verse 25: "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in line by the Spirit."

div.p: Stoichōmen ("let us walk in line, let us keep in step") is from stoicheō, whose root sense is standing in a row or rank — soldiers in formation, items in a column, elements in a series. It is the same root as stoicheia (4:3, 9), as systoichei ("corresponds to," 4:25), and as stoichēsousin ("as many as walk by this rule," 6:16). Four appearances of one root across three chapters, covering the elements that enslave, the column Hagar stands in, and the line believers are to keep.
The conditional ei ("if") is not doubtful but assumed: since we live by the Spirit — and 3:2-5 and 4:6 have established that they do — let our conduct fall into line with it.

The relation between the two halves is the section's whole logic. The indicative comes first and the imperative follows from it: they are told to become what they already are. That is the same structure as 5:1 (Christ set you free — therefore stand firm) and 5:13 (you were called to freedom — therefore serve one another).

p.hi: Verse 26: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another."

div.p: Kenodoxoi is a compound of kenos ("empty") and doxa ("glory, reputation") — seeking a glory with nothing inside it. The word appears only here in the New Testament, though the related noun kenodoxia appears at Philippians 2:3, also in a context about not putting oneself above others.

The two participles that follow are both reciprocal. Allēlous prokaloumenoi ("provoking one another") uses a verb meaning to call someone out, to challenge to a contest. Allēlois phthonountes ("envying one another") uses the verb behind phthonoi, one of the eight social vices at 5:21.

The section therefore ends where it began. It opened with the Galatians biting and devouring each other (5:15) and closes with them provoking and envying each other, using a word taken directly from the vice list in between. The theological crisis has produced a social one, and the instruction is aimed at that rather than at conduct in the abstract.

div.title: The Chapter's Argument as a Whole

list.item: The chapter states the cost of the conversion programme in the most direct language in the letter, and 5:3 explains why the stakes are so high. "I, Paul, say to you"; "Christ will be of no benefit"; "severed from Christ"; "fallen from grace." Nothing is hedged. And the reason is not that the law is bad but that circumcision is not an addition — it is enrolment in a covenant with its whole obligation, which is what proselyte conversion meant and what the other teachers appear to have obscured. The Izates story in Josephus shows the same argument being conducted among Jews, over an actual Gentile, in the same period.

The yoke image is not straightforwardly negative, and reading it as though it were flattens the verse. Jewish usage speaks of gladly taking up the yoke of the kingdom and of the commandments; Jesus offers a yoke that is "easy." Paul is inverting a positive image, and the inversion is carried by the genitive "of slavery." On the hardest comparison — Peter's unbearable yoke at Acts 15:10 — there is a real lexical link to Matthew 23:4, where the burden that is "hard to bear" is accumulated ruling rather than written Torah, and where the same verb is used for laying it on. That link is evidence; it is not proof, and it should not be presented as more than it is.

5:6 negates in both directions, and that is structurally decisive for reading the letter. "Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything." A position that simply opposed Jewish practice would need only half the sentence. What is denied is that either bodily state confers standing — and 6:15 repeats the formula in the same two-way form.

"Faith working through love" (5:6) rules out any reading in which faith is set against action as such. Energeō denotes actual operation and effect. The faith that counts is defined by what it does — by the same author, in the same letter, four verses after saying that seeking justification by law severs a man from Christ. An interpretation must hold both sentences without straining either.

The letter's hinge is 5:13, and it converts freedom into obligation. "Called to freedom... through love serve one another as slaves" — and the verb is douleuō, from the same root as the slavery Christ freed them from and as the enslavement of 2:4 and 4:3. Freedom here is not release from all service but release into a service that is given rather than exacted.

5:3 and 5:14 use different verbs of "the whole law" eleven verses apart, and the difference is the chapter's central datum. The proselyte is a debtor to do (poiēsai) the whole law; the whole law stands fulfilled (peplērōtai, perfect) in one word. And the summarizing move belongs to a recognized Jewish practice — Hillel, Jesus, Micah, and Paul himself at Romans 13:10 — in which the summary never means the remainder is discarded. Hillel's version ends "go and learn."

The vocabulary of 5:19 and 5:22 is deliberately unmatched, and the difference is doing work. Erga (plural) of the flesh, karpos (singular) of the Spirit. Works are produced by effort, are many, and can be counted and displayed — which is exactly what 6:13 says the other teachers want to do with the Galatians' bodies. Fruit is grown from a single source and is one thing with many aspects.

All of the chapter's warnings share one grammar, and it is worth noticing before a theology is imported. Severed from Christ and fallen out of grace (5:4); an inheritance not entered (5:21); and, in the next chapter, a harvest reaped only by those who do not give out (6:8-9). None describes a possession confiscated or a credit reversed. All describe a relation departed from or a destination not reached.

5:18 and 5:23 must be read together, and together they resist a simple law-versus-Spirit opposition. "If led by the Spirit, you are not under law" stands three verses before a list of behaviours that forfeit the kingdom, so it is not a release from obligation. And "against such things there is no law" says that what the Spirit produces is not what the law opposes. The letter is not setting the Spirit against the law's content; hypo nomon names a standing, and 4:4 is the control on the phrase.

The ethical material is aimed at a specific situation: these congregations are fighting each other. "Biting and devouring" (5:15); eight of the fifteen works of the flesh concerning communal breakdown; a closing warning about provoking and envying that reuses a word from the list (5:26). The theological crisis has become a social one, and the chapter's instruction addresses people who have started tearing at one another over it.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: Where this stands in the letter: Chapter 5 turned from argument to consequence at 5:13 and set the Spirit against the flesh. Chapter 6 carries that instruction into particular cases — what to do about someone who falls, how responsibility is shared and how it is not, what is owed to teachers, and what a life yields — and then closes.

The closing is different in kind from everything before it. At 6:11 Paul takes the pen from the scribe and writes the rest himself, drawing attention to the fact as he does so. What follows is a compressed restatement of the letter, composed by its author, in his own hand, after everything else has been said. That makes 6:11-18 unusually good evidence for what Paul took the letter to be about — better than any reader's summary, because it is his own.

Two structural observations about the ending, both unique to this letter. Every other letter of Paul closes with greetings, usually to named individuals and sometimes at length: Romans 16 names twenty-six people; Colossians 4:7-17 names ten and gives news of each. Galatians has none. No greeting to anyone, no news, no travel plans, no request for hospitality, no mention of a co-worker being sent or received, no "the churches of Asia greet you." And the letter that opened without a thanksgiving therefore also closes without greetings. Both silences are the author's own, and both are audible against his practice everywhere else.

What comes before (Galatians 5:13-26): The freedom argument turned into an obligation — "through love serve one another as slaves" — and the whole law was said to stand fulfilled in Leviticus 19:18. The works of the flesh were catalogued, with eight of the fifteen items concerning conflict inside a group, and the fruit of the Spirit was named as a single crop. The section closed on the Galatians provoking and envying one another (5:26), after an earlier warning that they were biting and devouring each other (5:15).

Chapter 6 opens by addressing a congregation in exactly that condition. Its first instruction is about how to handle someone who has fallen, and its first named virtue is gentleness. Neither is an accident of arrangement.

div.title: Verses 1-5: Burdens and Loads

div.p: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness. Watch yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will bear his own load.

p.hi: Verse 1a: "Brothers, if anyone is caught in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness."

div.p: Ean kai prolēmphthē anthrōpos en tini paraptōmati. The verb prolambanō means "to take beforehand," and in the passive "to be caught, overtaken, surprised, detected." Two senses are available and the Greek does not choose between them.
On the first, the man is caught by the trespass — overtaken by it, surprised into it before he saw it coming. This is the more sympathetic reading and it fits the gentleness that follows.
On the second, he is caught in it — discovered, found out by others. This is the more forensic reading and it fits a congregation in which people are watching each other.
Both produce the same instruction, which may be why Paul did not disambiguate.

Paraptōma is worth distinguishing from its near-neighbour. It is built on piptō, "to fall," with para-, "beside" — a false step, a slip, a stumble off the path. Paul's other word, parabasis (used at 2:18 and 3:19), is built on bainō, "to go," with para- — a deliberate stepping across a stated line. Paraptōma is the gentler of the two, and it is the one Paul chose here. Whatever has happened, it is described as a fall rather than a defiance.

The indefinite pronouns are generous: anthrōpos ("a person," not "one of you") and en tini paraptōmati ("in any trespass"). No category of fall is excluded from the instruction, and no category of person.
Hymeis hoi pneumatikoi ("you who are spiritual") picks up from 5:25 — those who live by the Spirit and walk in line with it.

Whether this addresses a subgroup within the congregation or the whole of it is not stated, and the question has been read both ways. Some have heard irony in it, as though Paul were quoting a self-designation back at people who claimed it. Against that: the letter has consistently addressed all of these congregations as possessing the Spirit — they received it (3:2-5), the Spirit of the Son is in their hearts crying Abba (4:6), they are led by the Spirit (5:18) and live by the Spirit (5:25). On the letter's own terms, "you who are spiritual" describes the readers as such. Reading it as a barb requires importing a tone the letter has not established.

Katartizete ("restore") is the key word of the section, and the image behind it does the work. Katartizō means "to put in order, to mend, to repair, to make fit, to bring to a proper condition." Its uses are concrete before they are figurative:

list.item: It is what James and John were doing to their nets when they were called — "in the boat mending (katartizontas) their nets" (Mark 1:19; Matthew 4:21). A torn net is useless and is not thrown away; it is repaired and put back in the water.
In medical Greek it is the standard word for setting a broken bone — restoring the limb to its proper alignment so that it can bear weight again.
It covers refitting a ship, and equipping a person for a task (the cognate noun appears at Ephesians 4:12, "for the equipping of the saints").

div.p: What these share is the return of something to working order. The instruction is therefore not to discipline, to exclude, or to correct doctrinally — and it is not merely to forgive. It is to mend, and mending assumes both that the thing is worth the trouble and that it is expected to function again.

En pneumati prautētos ("in a spirit of gentleness"). Prautēs is among the fruit listed at 5:23, and the word does not mean weakness. In Greek usage it describes strength that is under control — it is used of a horse that has been broken, which has lost none of its power and has gained a rider. Moses is called the meekest man on earth (Numbers 12:3) in the middle of a book in which he confronts Pharaoh and the people repeatedly.
The manner prescribed for mending is thus drawn directly from what the Spirit was said to grow, which ties the instruction to the preceding chapter rather than beginning something new.

p.hi: Verse 1b: "Watch yourself, lest you too be tempted."

div.p: Skopōn seauton shifts abruptly to the singular, mid-sentence, after a plural address. The generalized instruction to a community becomes a warning to each individual who acts on it.

Skopeō is "to look at, to keep an eye on, to fix one's attention on" — the verb behind "scope" and "telescope." The attention that was directed at the fallen man is to be turned back on the one directing it.
Mē kai sy peirasthēs ("lest you also be tempted"). The word peirazō covers both testing and tempting; the noun peirasmos appeared at 4:14 for the trial Paul's illness posed to the Galatians.

The clause concedes something that the whole enterprise of restoration depends on: the one doing the mending stands in the same exposure as the one being mended. Nothing in the instruction places him above it, and the change to the singular makes the point personally rather than as a general maxim.

p.hi: Verse 2: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

div.p: Allēlōn ta barē bastazete. Baros is a weight — something heavy, and in figurative use something oppressive, a load that presses down. Paul uses it at 1 Thessalonians 2:7 of the weight an apostle could have thrown around, and at 2 Corinthians 4:17 of an "eternal weight of glory."

Bastazō is "to carry, to bear, to take up and hold." It is the verb of 5:10 ("he will bear the judgment"), and it will appear twice more in this chapter — at 6:5 of one's own load, and at 6:17 of the marks Paul carries on his body. Four uses in two chapters, of a judgment, a burden, a load, and a set of scars.

Ton nomon tou Christou ("the law of Christ") appears only here in the Pauline letters, and its closest relative is 1 Corinthians 9:21, where Paul describes himself as "not being without law toward God but ennomos Christou" — within Christ's law, in-lawed to Christ. That passage is instructive because it is also a passage about accommodation: Paul says he became as one under law to those under law, and as one outside law to those outside it, and inserts this phrase to forestall the conclusion that he is therefore lawless.

p.hi: The phrase here is not defined, but the sentence supplies what fulfils it, and that is a substantial constraint on any definition.

div.p: What fulfils the law of Christ is carrying each other's weight. Not believing something, not belonging to something, not observing something. That places the phrase in direct relation to 5:14, where "the whole law is fulfilled in one word: you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Bearing burdens is Leviticus 19:18 performed rather than recited.
Three readings of what the phrase denotes are available, and the letter does not decide among them:

A new code given by Christ, replacing or superseding the Torah. This reading has the difficulty that the letter nowhere sets out such a code, and that when Paul does state the content of what is to be fulfilled, at 5:14, he quotes Leviticus.

The Torah as read and embodied by Christ — the same instruction, seen through the one who fully performed it. This reading fits 5:14 comfortably, and fits the fact that the "law of Christ" is fulfilled by doing what Leviticus 19:18 commands.

The pattern of Christ's own conduct functioning as a norm. The one thing this letter says Christ did is give himself for others — "who gave himself for our sins" (1:4), "who loved me and gave himself for me" (2:20). Bearing what is not yours to bear is precisely that pattern, and on this reading 6:2 says: do what he did.

The readings are not sharply exclusive, and a reader should notice that most commentaries answer the question on grounds imported from elsewhere in the New Testament rather than from anything Galatians says.

Anaplērōsete ("you will fill up completely") is a strengthened form of the plēroō used at 5:14, with ana- adding the sense of filling right to the top. Some manuscripts have the imperative ("fulfil!") rather than the future ("you will fulfil"); the difference is slight, since a future indicative in this position functions much like a command.

p.hi: Verses 3-4: "For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor."

div.p: The connection to verse 2 runs through what obstructs it. A man who thinks himself something will not stoop to carry another man's weight. Self-assessment is therefore not a change of subject; it is the condition of the instruction just given.

Phrenapata heauton ("he deceives his own mind") is a compound of phrēn ("mind, understanding, the seat of thought") and apataō ("to deceive"), found nowhere else in the New Testament and rare in Greek generally. The deception is located in the understanding rather than in the will — the man is not lying; he has fooled himself.

The construction is stark: dokei tis einai ti mēden ōn — "if anyone supposes himself to be something, being nothing." The two indefinite pronouns, ti ("something") and mēden ("nothing"), are set directly against each other with no qualification.

Dokimazetō ("let him test, examine, prove") is the verb for assaying metal — putting a sample to fire or to the touchstone to determine whether it is genuine and what its content is. The related adjective dokimos means "tested and approved," and adokimos "failed the test, rejected." Paul uses the verb of self-examination at 1 Corinthians 11:28 and 2 Corinthians 13:5.
The object is to ergon heautou, "his own work" — singular, the whole of what a man does rather than a selection from it.

Kauchēma ("boast, ground of boasting") is the noun. It anticipates the closing section, where boasting is at issue twice: what the other teachers want to boast in (6:13), and what Paul will boast in (6:14).

The instruction is that any ground of confidence must come from examining one's own work — eis heauton monon kai ouk eis ton heteron, "with reference to himself alone and not to the other." What is being ruled out is the comparative: confidence built by measuring oneself against a neighbour rather than against the work itself. In a congregation described as provoking and envying one another (5:26), this is not an abstract caution.

p.hi: Verse 5: "For each will bear his own load."
The apparent contradiction with verse 2 dissolves in the Greek, because two different nouns are used, and the difference is not subtle.

div.p: Verse 2: bear one another's barē. A weight, and in this context an oppressive one — the thing that presses a person down and that he cannot manage alone.

Verse 5: each will bear his own phortion. A phortion is a consignment — a ship's cargo, a pack assigned to a soldier or a porter, a merchant's freight. It is what a person is properly given to carry, sized to him and belonging to him. It is the same noun Jesus uses at Matthew 11:30: "my burden (phortion) is light."
The verb is identical in both verses — bastazō — so the entire distinction rests on the nouns, which is exactly how a Greek reader would have taken it.

The two instructions are therefore complementary and not in tension. Help with what crushes; carry what is assigned. The first concerns someone else's crisis; the second concerns your own responsibility, and neither cancels the other.

The future tense (bastasei, "will bear") may be a general future — this is how things are — or may look toward a final accounting, which would fit the sowing-and-reaping material immediately following.

div.title: Verses 6-10: Sowing and Reaping

div.p: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith.

p.hi: Verse 6: "Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches."

div.p: Koinōneitō is the verb of koinōnia — to have in common, to share, to participate, to go partners in something. It is the same root as the "fellowship" of the handshake at 2:9, where Paul and Barnabas were given "the right hand of koinōnia."

Ho katechoumenos ("the one being instructed") is the passive participle of katēcheō, "to instruct orally" — built on ēcheō, "to sound," so literally to sound something down into someone. The English words "catechumen" and "catechism" descend from it, and the verb's presence here is evidence that these congregations had settled arrangements for teaching, with recognized teachers.
En pasin agathois ("in all good things") means goods and not sentiments. The instruction is that those who receive instruction should support those who give it, materially.

Paul addresses the same obligation at much greater length at 1 Corinthians 9:3-14, where he argues it from four directions — the soldier who does not pay his own wages, the vine-dresser who eats the fruit, the shepherd who drinks the milk, and the Torah's own ruling that "you shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain" (Deuteronomy 25:4) — and then declines to make use of the right himself.

Why the instruction appears here, between a warning about self-assessment and a warning about sowing, is not stated. The connection may simply be practical: a congregation in conflict is a congregation whose teachers go unsupported.

p.hi: Verse 7: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."

div.p: Mē planasthe ("do not be led astray") is from planaō, "to cause to wander" — the root of "planet," the wandering star. Paul uses this exact formula elsewhere to head off a mistaken assumption (1 Corinthians 6:9; 15:33), and its presence signals that what follows corrects something people are inclined to think.

Theos ou myktērizetai ("God is not sneered at"). Myktērizō is built on myktēr, "nostril," and means literally to turn up the nose at someone — to treat with open and visible contempt. The Greek scriptures use it of contempt for wisdom and for the righteous: "they despised all my reproof" (Proverbs 1:30); "a foolish son mocks his father" (Proverbs 15:20); "the righteous see it and are glad; the innocent laugh them to scorn" (Job 22:19).

The passive with God as its subject is the point. God is not the sort of thing that can be treated with contempt and not notice. The sense is not that God takes offence at insults but that the arrangement being described cannot be gamed — one cannot appear to satisfy it while doing otherwise and expect the appearance to hold.
The sowing-and-reaping principle is proverbial and runs throughout the scriptures, always with the same two components:

list.item: "Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity" (Proverbs 22:8)
"Those who plough iniquity and sow trouble reap the same" (Job 4:8)
"They sow the wind and they shall reap the whirlwind" (Hosea 8:7)
"Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap the fruit of steadfast love" (Hosea 10:12)
"Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" (Psalm 126:5)

div.p: The two components are *correspondence* and *delay*. What comes up is the kind of thing that went into the ground — a farmer does not sow barley and reap wheat. And the harvest does not arrive with the sowing; there is a season in between during which nothing visible happens and the sower has only his own work to go on. Both components are operative in the verses that follow: verse 8 states the correspondence, verse 9 states the delay.

p.hi: Verse 8: "For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life."

div.p: The flesh-and-Spirit contrast of 5:16-26 is restated agriculturally, and the restatement makes it a matter of outcome rather than of struggle.

Eis tēn sarka heautou ("into his own flesh") — the reflexive is emphatic. Sowing into the flesh is sowing into oneself, which is a fair description of the vice list at 5:19-21, where more than half the items concern a person's advancement at the expense of the group.

Phthora ("corruption, decay, ruin, perishing") is what happens to perishable things by their nature — the word covers rot, spoilage, and destruction. Paul uses it of the created order's bondage at Romans 8:21 and of what is sown perishable at 1 Corinthians 15:42. The point of the word is that no external punishment needs to be added: what is sown into the perishable yields according to its kind.

Zōēn aiōnion ("life of the age") is the standard expression for the life of the age to come. It belongs to the two-age framework the letter announced in its greeting — deliverance "out of the present evil age" (1:4) — and it is the only occurrence of the phrase in this letter.

The structure of the claim deserves attention because it is easy to read past. Both harvests use the same verb (therisei) in the same tense, and both follow from what was sown. Eternal life is stated here as a crop reaped, which is to say as something arrived at rather than something held from the beginning and merely retained.

That is the same grammar the letter has used throughout for what is at stake: a connection severed and a position fallen out of (5:4), an inheritance not entered (5:21), a harvest reaped or not (6:8). None of these describes a possession confiscated or a credit reversed. All describe something departed from, not arrived at, or not brought in.

p.hi: Verse 9: "And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up."

div.p: Mē enkakōmen ("let us not lose heart, grow weary in, become discouraged"). The compound is en- plus kakos, "bad" — to behave badly in the sense of flagging, to turn faint-hearted at a task.
To kalon poiountes ("doing the good") uses kalos, which means good in the sense of fine, admirable, worthy — what looks right and is right.

Kairō gar idiō therisomen ("for in its own season we shall reap"). The delay component of the proverb is stated plainly. Kairos is not clock-time (chronos) but the right time, the appointed moment, the season proper to a thing. A harvest has one, and it is not chosen by the farmer.

Mē ekluomenoi ("not fainting, not giving out") is from ekluō, "to loose out, to unloose, to let go slack." It is used of collapsing from hunger (Matthew 15:32), of the strength going out of a person, of a bowstring going slack.

The conditional is explicit and Paul does not soften it. The harvest comes in its season if we do not give out. The sentence is built as a promise with a condition attached, and both halves are stated.

The pastoral situation this addresses is visible in the verse itself. Between sowing and reaping there is a season in which nothing appears to be happening, and the temptation in that season is not to do evil but to stop doing good because it seems to yield nothing. That is what enkakeō and ekluō both describe.

p.hi: Verse 10: "So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith."

div.p: Hōs kairon echomen ("as we have opportunity") plays on the kairō idiō of the previous verse. There is a season for reaping, which is not now, and a season for working, which is. The word is the same; the two seasons are different.

Ergazōmetha to agathon ("let us work the good") — the verb is ergazomai, from ergon, the noun that has appeared throughout the letter in "works of law" (2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) and "works of the flesh" (5:19). Here the same root is used positively and without qualification: work the good.

Tous oikeious tēs pisteōs ("those of the household of faith") uses oikeios, "belonging to the house," from oikos. The word describes family members and dependents as distinct from outsiders, and it continues the household imagery that has run from 4:1-7 (heir, guardians, stewards, adoption) through 4:19 (little children) to here.

The scope is stated as a priority, not as a restriction. Pros pantas — to all. Malista de — especially, to these. The nearer obligation does not withdraw the wider one, and a reader should notice that the verse is often quoted with only its second half.

div.title: Verses 11-18: The Postscript in Paul's Own Hand

div.p: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand! It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would compel you to be circumcised — only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh. But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

p.hi: Verse 11: "See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand!"

div.p: The convention behind this needs stating for the sentence to register. Letters in this period were normally dictated to a trained scribe, who wrote in a small, practised, even hand. Romans 16:22 preserves such a scribe's own greeting, inserted into the letter: "I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord."

The sender would commonly add a closing in his own hand, both as authentication and as a personal touch: "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand" (1 Corinthians 16:21); "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand" (Colossians 4:18); "I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it" (Philemon 19). At 2 Thessalonians 3:17 the practice is explicitly described as a security measure: "this is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write."
Here Paul draws attention both to the change of hand and to the size of his letters. Pēlikois... grammasin — "with what large characters."

Why they are large is not stated, and the proposals are all reconstructions: poor eyesight, which some connect to 4:15 and the offer of the Galatians' eyes; unfamiliarity with the pen in a man who normally dictated; hands coarsened by manual labour (Paul worked with his hands, 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 4:12) or damaged by the beatings referred to at 6:17; or simple emphasis — writing large the way a person raises his voice, so that what follows cannot be skimmed.

What does not depend on the explanation is the status of what follows. From verse 11 to the end, this is the author's own hand and his own summary, set down after everything else has been said. What he chooses to restate is therefore evidence of a kind not otherwise available.

p.hi: Verse 12: "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would compel you to be circumcised — only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ."

div.p: Euprosōpēsai en sarki ("to put on a good face in the flesh"). The verb is a compound of eu ("well") and prosōpon ("face"), found nowhere else in the New Testament and rare in Greek generally. It denotes making a good outward appearance — looking right to observers, presenting a face that will pass inspection.
The phrase en sarki does the double duty it has done throughout the letter: a good showing in the outward and visible sphere, and a good showing measured in circumcised bodies.

Anankazousin ("they compel") is the verb of 2:3 (Titus, who was not compelled) and 2:14 (Peter, compelling Gentiles to Judaize). Its three occurrences in this letter all concern pressure applied to Gentiles about circumcision, and together they form a set that spans the whole document.
The motive Paul assigns them is the avoidance of persecution, and the sentence is emphatic about it: monon hina — "only in order that" — tō staurō tou Christou mē diōkōntai.

What that persecution would have consisted of, and why circumcising Gentile converts would avert it. The letter does not explain, and any account is reconstruction, but the situation it presupposes is intelligible and worth setting out, because without it the verse is opaque.

A Gentile in a Greek or Roman city was expected to participate in the cults of his household, his trade association, and his city. This was not private religion in a modern sense; it was civic and social obligation, woven into public festivals, guild dinners, family observances and civic loyalty. A Gentile who stopped participating was conspicuous and was liable to be regarded as antisocial or disloyal.

Jewish communities had long-established customary allowances for their own non-participation, recognized in practice by Roman authorities. A Gentile who converted and became a Jew moved into that recognized position. A Gentile who joined a Jewish-derived movement but did not convert occupied no recognized position at all: he had abandoned the cults without entering the community whose abstention was tolerated.

There is also pressure to be reckoned from the other direction. A movement that proclaimed a crucified man as Messiah and admitted uncircumcised Gentiles as full members without conversion was liable to bring trouble on the Jewish communities associated with it — and on any Jewish teachers identified with it.
On either account, circumcising the Gentile converts regularizes an anomaly, and it does so at their expense rather than at the teachers' own.

This connects directly to 5:11, where Paul argued from his own persecution that he cannot be preaching circumcision. The two verses are the two ends of one argument: preaching a cross sufficient without conversion draws persecution; adding conversion removes it.

A caution that should be entered plainly and not buried. This is Paul's characterization of his opponents' motives, and it is not their account of themselves. This letter is the only surviving source for the dispute. The other party left no writing; we do not have their reasoning, their scriptural arguments, or their self-understanding, and we do not know whether they would have recognized the motive attributed to them here. A reader should hold this verse with that awareness — not as a reason to disbelieve Paul, but as a fact about the evidence.

p.hi: Verse 13: "For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh."

div.p: Hoi peritemnomenoi is a present participle, and its referent is genuinely disputed. The form may be middle or passive, and it can be rendered "those who are circumcised" (a settled state), "those who are getting circumcised" (in process), or "those who have themselves circumcised."
Three candidates follow.
The other teachers, as circumcised men — Jews pressing a requirement they were born into. This is the simplest reading, though it strains the present tense somewhat.

The Galatians themselves, currently in the process of accepting it. This fits the present tense but makes the sentence awkward: Paul would be saying that the Galatians do not keep the law, which is trivially true of men who have only just started.

The other teachers as themselves recent proselytes — Gentiles who converted and now recruit others. This gives the present participle its full force and would explain several things at once: the eagerness to make converts, the possibility of "boasting" in a tally of them, and a convert's characteristic zeal for the boundary he has just crossed. It is a reconstruction, not a demonstration, and the text does not confirm it.
Nomon phylassousin ("they keep the law"). Phylassō is "to guard, to keep watch over, to observe" — the standard verb for keeping commandments in the Greek scriptures.
The charge that those pressing the programme do not perform it can be heard in two ways, and they are quite different.
As hypocrisy: they demand of others what they do not do themselves. This is the ordinary reading and it is a charge about character.

As an argument that the programme is incoherent: the covenant being urged is not in fact being kept by those urging it, so what precisely is on offer? On this reading the point is structural rather than personal, and it draws on 5:3 — circumcision obligates a man to the whole law, and if the whole is not being kept by anyone in view, then the transaction does not deliver what it advertises.

Hina en tē hymetera sarki kauchēsōntai ("that they may boast in your flesh") supplies the alternative motive to that of verse 12. Converts as a record of achievement — countable, displayable, and made of other people's bodies. The possessive is pointed: your flesh, their boast.

p.hi: Verse 14: "But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."

div.p: Emoi de mē genoito kauchasthai uses the letter's strongest negation, mē genoito, which appeared at 2:17 and 3:21 to reject an inference drawn from Paul's position. Here it rejects a possibility about himself.

Boasting is not a marginal theme in the scriptures Paul is working from. Jeremiah 9:23-24 sets the terms: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches; but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me." Paul quotes that passage twice (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17). The question is never whether to boast but in what.

Paul's answer is the cross — which, as an object of boasting, is a deliberate outrage. Crucifixion was a slave's death and a rebel's death, designed to humiliate; Roman writers of the period treat it as barely mentionable. To name it as one's sole ground of boasting is to invert the entire economy of honour that the phrase "make a good showing" (v. 12) belongs to.

Di' hou emoi kosmos estaurōtai kagō kosmō ("through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world"). Both verbs are perfect — completed action with standing result — and the severance runs in both directions. Not merely that Paul has withdrawn from the world's estimation, but that the world has been put to death with respect to him. Neither party is any longer in a position to make claims on the other.

Kosmos here names the present ordering of things — the same register as "the present evil age" (1:4) and "the elements of the world" (4:3). It is not the created order as such but the world as a system of value, standing and appearance, which is exactly what verse 12's "good showing" belongs to.

The three crucifixion statements in the letter now stand together: "I have been crucified with Christ" (2:19-20); "those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh" (5:24); "the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (6:14). In each case the severance is decisive, and in each case it is participatory in a death that was not the speaker's own.

p.hi: Verse 15: "For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation."

div.p: The first half repeats 5:6 in substance; the second half differs. Where 5:6 had "faith working through love," this has kainē ktisis, "new creation."

Note again that the negation runs both ways. Uncircumcision counts no more than circumcision. Whatever the letter is arguing against, it is not Jewish practice as such but the assignment of standing to a bodily condition — and the sentence rules out both directions with equal force.

p.hi: The phrase kainē ktisis admits two readings, and the letter supports both. Neither should be presented as settled.

div.p: Reading one: the renewed order. Ktisis is the standard word for the created order or for the act of creating. Paul uses it that way at Romans 8:19-22, where "the whole creation groans" and awaits its liberation from corruption. On this reading, kainē ktisis names the new age into which the present one is giving way — and the letter would then close where it opened, since 1:4 announced deliverance "out of the present evil age." The inclusio would be deliberate.

Two further supports: the immediately preceding verse has just had a world crucified, which is a cosmic statement rather than a personal one; and the letter's whole frame, from 1:4 through the stoicheia of 4:3 and 4:9, is a two-age frame.

Reading two: the person made new. The contrast within the sentence is with a bodily alteration — circumcision, uncircumcision — which makes an inward or personal renewal an apt antithesis: not a change made to the body but a change in what the person is. The natural parallel is 2 Corinthians 5:17, "if anyone is in Christ, new creation; the old things passed away, behold, they have become new" — where the Greek supplies neither a verb nor a pronoun ("he is a new creation" is a translator's addition) and which is itself read both ways.

The two are not mutually exclusive: a person made new may be the first instance of a renewal that is wider than himself, and Romans 8:19-23 sets the two side by side. The verse does not adjudicate, and readers should notice when a translation has adjudicated for them by supplying "he is."

p.hi: Verse 16: "And as for all who walk by this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God."

div.p: Hosoi tō kanoni toutō stoichēsousin ("as many as will walk in line by this rule").

Kanon is a measuring rod, a straight-edge, a rule in the carpenter's sense — the standard against which straightness is judged. The English "canon" descends from it. Stoicheō is the verb of 5:25, from the root that has appeared as stoicheia (4:3, 9) and systoichei (4:25): to stand in a row, to keep formation, to walk in line.
"This rule" most naturally refers to what was just said in verse 15.

p.hi: Kai epi ton Israēl tou theou ("and upon the Israel of God") is the most contested phrase in the letter, and the dispute turns entirely on the conjunction kai.

div.p: Read epexegetically — "and that is to say, upon the Israel of God" — the phrase identifies the group just named, those who walk by this rule, as the Israel of God. This has been the dominant reading in the interpretive tradition, and it is the reading most English translations imply by their punctuation.
Read additively — "and also upon the Israel of God" — it names a second group receiving the same blessing alongside the first.

p.hi: Three considerations bear on the choice, and they should be laid out rather than assumed.

div.p: First, kai is normally additive. That is its ordinary function and what a reader meeting it would expect. The epexegetic use ("and indeed," "that is to say") is well attested and genuinely available, but it is the marked, less common sense. It has to be argued for from context; it cannot simply be asserted, and the burden of proof lies on the party invoking it.

Second, there is no external usage to appeal to. The phrase Israēl tou theou occurs nowhere else — not in the Greek scriptures, not in surviving Jewish writings of the period, not elsewhere in the New Testament, not in any Greek text that has come down to us. There is no established sense to consult.

And Paul uses Israēl roughly sixteen times across his letters — including the sustained argument of Romans 9-11, where an enormous amount turns on the word, and where he distinguishes carefully between Israel and the Gentiles being grafted in — without ever unambiguously applying it to a mixed or Gentile body.

Third, the sentence has the shape of a synagogue benediction. The closing blessing of the Amidah, the central prayer of Jewish worship, asks God to grant "peace, goodness and blessing, grace and lovingkindness and mercy, upon us and upon all Israel your people." Galatians 6:16 runs: peace upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God — the same elements, in the same order, ending in the same tail.

The Amidah's fixed wording is later than Paul, so this is a formal parallel and not a demonstrable citation. But the form of such a blessing is old, and if a familiar liturgical closing is in view, then "and upon Israel" is a formula — and a formula is not the kind of thing that gets silently redefined halfway through its own recitation.

None of this settles the verse, and it would be dishonest to present it as settling it. What the evidence does show is that the additive reading is not the eccentric one, and that the epexegetic reading carries a burden of proof it is frequently not made to bear. A reader should take a position here knowingly, and should notice when a commentary, a translation's punctuation, or a sermon has taken one without saying that a choice was made.

p.hi: Verse 17: "From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus."

div.p: Tou loipou ("from now on, henceforth, for the rest") signals a final word on the matter.

Kopous moi mēdeis parechetō ("let no one furnish troubles to me"). Kopos is labour, trouble, wearisome effort — the noun behind kopiaō, the verb Paul used at 4:11 for having laboured over the Galatians to exhaustion. The idiom "to furnish trouble to someone" appears at Matthew 26:10 and Luke 11:7.

Ta stigmata tou Iēsou ("the marks of Jesus"). A stigma is a brand or a tattoo — a mark cut or burnt into the skin, permanent and visible. Its uses in this world were specific and they were all about ownership or allegiance:

list.item: Slaves were branded, both to show whose they were and to make runaways identifiable and unsaleable.
Soldiers in some contexts bore marks of their unit or their commander.
Devotees of certain deities bore marks identifying whose they were, which is attested in several cults of the period.

div.p: In every case the mark answered the question: whose is this man?
Bastazō ("I bear") is the verb of 6:2 and 6:5, and of Acts 15:10.

What the marks were. Paul catalogues them at 2 Corinthians 11:23-25: "far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death. Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned." A man who had survived that carried it on his skin permanently.

p.hi: The placement of this sentence is the letter's final argument, and it contains no theology at all.

div.p: The entire letter has been a dispute about a mark made in the flesh and about what that mark proves. Paul closes by producing a different mark, in his own flesh. It was not chosen, it was not applied in a ceremony, and it confers no status. It is what happened to a man who preached the cross without the rite — and it answers the same question circumcision was being offered to answer.
The counterpart to circumcision, in other words, turns out not to be another rite. It is scar tissue.

p.hi: Verse 18: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen."

div.p: The benediction is standard in its opening — charis, "grace," is the word the letter began with at 1:3 and the sphere the Galatians were called into at 1:6 and were said to have fallen out of at 5:4. The letter ends by wishing them the thing it warned them they were leaving.
Two departures from Paul's usual form.
Meta tou pneumatos hymōn ("with your spirit") rather than the more usual "with you all." The same form appears at Philippians 4:23 and Philemon 25.
Adelphoi ("brothers") stands at the very end — after the benediction, immediately before the Amen. It occupies that position in no other Pauline letter.

The placement is worth registering, and it is the last thing the letter does. This document contains "I am astonished"; "you foolish Galatians"; "who has bewitched you"; "let him be accursed," twice; "you are severed from Christ"; "you have fallen from grace"; "I am afraid I have laboured over you in vain"; and "I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves."
Its final word before the Amen is brothers.

Nothing in six chapters has withdrawn that address. The severity throughout is aimed at a movement the writer believes can still be reversed — the desertion is in progress at 1:6, the circumcision has not yet happened at 5:2, and the confidence at 5:10 is that they will come round — and the relationship the letter is written from does not change from the first line to the last.

Amen transliterates the Hebrew 'amen, from a root meaning firmness or reliability. It is the word by which a congregation assents to what has been said and makes it its own — which means the letter ends by inviting the people it has just rebuked to say yes to it.

div.title: The Chapter's Argument as a Whole

list.item: The instruction of 6:1-5 is addressed to a congregation that has been described as biting and devouring one another (5:15) and provoking and envying one another (5:26). The verb for dealing with someone who has fallen is katartizō — to mend a net, to set a bone, to restore a thing to working order — and the manner prescribed is gentleness, taken from the list of what the Spirit grows. Neither the word nor the manner is chosen at random for a congregation in that condition.

The one doing the restoring is warned, in the singular, that he stands in the same exposure. The abrupt change from plural to singular mid-sentence makes the warning personal rather than general.
